former Head, Architecture & Civil Engineering Division, BARC) to monitor and troubleshoot major
issues, and assist the director on matters related to permanent campus development project. This
team regularly (bi-weekly) meets with key parties (CPWD, ITDC and Sikka Associates) to identify
any issues related to their work. It also proposes action plan to address the issues at hand so that
target deadlines are met.

deliverables for quality. QMC comprises of members from institute administration and external
experts.

IIT Ropar Annual Report 2014-1576
22.1 ZEITGEIST
This year zeitgeist was a tremendous success. The event lasted for 2 days and 3 nights. It was filled
with jubilant cultural events like dance, music, singing competitions and fashion show. The event
recorded a footfall of more than 5000. This festival was enriched by three pro-nights. The first night
saw the mind boggling performances of “astitva the band” and the “sunburn campus starring DJ
Avtar”. The crowd danced their souls out during these performances. The second night saw the
performance of “the local train band”.
22.2 LOHRI
This festival is celebrated in Punjab as Lohri and in Gujarat /Maharashtra as Makar Sankranti. This
year lohri was celebrated in a festive manner. A bonfire was arranged near mercury hostel. All the
students gathered and sang ritual songs. Students had sweets and dryfruits and danced.
22.3 HOLI
The festival of colors was celebrated at IIT Ropar in a great way. Students enjoyed sweets and colors
arranged by the institute. People played with colors and water and enjoyed the ambience.
22.4 INTER-BATCH CULTURAL CHAMPIONSHIP
Inter-Batch Cultural festival was organized very first time at IIT Ropar. It was like a mini Zeitgeist.
There were many cultural events. Teams from each batch prepared performances and participated
in the competition. This was the first event to find the cultural talent of our institute. The students of
2011 batch won the maiden general championship.
22.5 CULTURAL NIGHT
Cultural night was organized in October as a farewell to final year students. The event was to show
the cultural talent of students by various dance, dramatics, singing performances. The students bid
adieu to final year with emotions and sentiments.
22.6 INTER IIT SPORTS MEET 2014
A contingent of strength-91 participated in the inter IIT sports meet held at IIT Bombay in
December, 2014. IIT Ropar participated in various events like cricket, football, basketball,
badminton, etc. IIT Ropar participated with good spirit.
22.7 INTER YEAR SPORTS TOURNAMENT
A sports tournament with 5 teams (one for each year and PhD) was organised. It was the first time,
when a separate team of PhD participated in this tournament. Various games were played and the
PhD team bagged the trophy.
22.8 CRICKET LEAGUE – PPL
A cricket league was arranged on the basis of IPL. Cricket players from all the batches come forward
and made 4 icon players to play the part of the manager of the team. An auction was conducted and 4
teams were formed. A trophy was given to the winning team.
22.9 MIXED MATCHES
Various other interesting and fun sport events were also organized throughout the year that
includes games like basketball, table tennis, volley ball etc.
22. STUDENTS ACTIVITIES

23.1 INTRODUCTION
Central Library of IIT Ropar plays a pivotal role in support of academic and research activities of the
Institute with the main functions of acquiring, processing, preserving and dissemination of print
and electronic resources. The objective of the library is to provide its user the required information
resources such as text-books, reference books, handbooks, encyclopedias, dictionaries, Journals,
magazines etc with appropriate delivery systems and services in order to support the institute to
achieve excellence in teaching and learning, learning, research and community service. Library is
also aiming to provide advanced level research support services.
23.2 COLLECTION DEVELOPMENT
Collection building is one of the important functions of the library, which supports academic and
research activities of the students, faculty, staff and other users.
The Library is continuously developing collection by acquiring latest books, journals, reports and
other reference and information resource materials in science, engineering, technology, humanities
and social sciences during the year. The Library is holding an excellent print collection of over
12000 documents which includes various resources such as dictionaries, handbooks,
encyclopedias, reports of research monographs, multi-volume reference works etc.. Apart from
this, the library holds a growing collection of CDs/DVDs, electronic journals, annual reports,
standards and pamphlets in areas of science, engineering, technology, humanities and social
sciences. In the financial year 2014-15, the library added 1370 new books to its collection.
23.3 ELECTRONIC RESOURCES
The Central Library facilitates online access to thousands of electronic journals through direct
subscription and participation in consortia, such as INDEST-AICTE and UGC-INFLIBNET
consortium. The library also provides online access to citations and scientometric database such as
Scopus and MathSciNet. The library provides access to the following publishers' Electronic
Resources.

IIT Ropar Annual Report 2014-15 81
24.1 GUEST HOUSE
The Institute's guest house is conveniently situated adjoining the residential area of the
campus. It is a very pleasant place for the institute's guests spanning across academia to
institute's alumni and parents of the institute’s students. Just a two minute walk from the main
gate of the campus, this soothing residence is surrounded by a lush green garden with a
badminton court to keep a person hale and healthy.
Guest house has three different categories of accommodation. The main guest house has six
rooms with en suite facilities, garden, badminton court etc., while the guest house no. 3 has
three rooms and the guest house no. 5 has three rooms, along with lounge and dining facilities
for special lunch for special occasion. All the rooms of the guesthouse are equipped with
standard amenities such as broadband connectivity, TV, AC etc.
24.2 MEDICAL CENTER
The Institute has medical center adjacent to hostel complex with 12 hours OPD. To attend any
medical emergency of the campus, a doctor, a pharmacist and a nurse are available 24x7.
Facilities of ECG, NIBP, oxygen saturation, blood sugar monitor and Fetal hearts Doppler
monitor are provided for students, staff and faculty members. Various new drugs, antibiotics
and medical devices (autoscope, X- ray illuminator, digital bp monitor,dressing trolley,digital
weighing scale) are introduced. Ee-Awareness of various contagious and non contagious
diseases and various alerts and preventive measures started through emails. Currently, there
are three drivers for 24x7 ambulance service.
24.3 HOUSING FACILITIES
IIT Ropar campus has 46 apartments in one or two storey buildings. There are 18 flats with
1000 sq. ft. area, 12 flats of 600 sft., 12 flats of 400 sq.ft. and 4 bungalows of 1300 sq.ft. for
residence of officials, faculty and staff. Round the clock security, power, DG back up and water
facilities are provided in residential area. The campus has 100 mbps dedicated internet line
serving residential area also. The residential buildings are surrounded by children play area
and parking facilities.
24.4 BANK
State Bank of India, IIT Ropar was established on 21-08-2009, to assist and take care of the
financial requirements of students, staff and faculty members. The branch caters to needs of
saving bank A/C, RD, FD, Loans (Car, Personal) insurance (life & general) Mutual funds etc. on a
day to day basis. The working hours of the branch are from 10 am to 4 pm from Monday to
Friday and 10 am to 1 pm on Saturdays. The business of the branch is approx. 70.92 crores as on
30/6/15. Since its inception, the branch has delicately supported and sincerely operated in its
functions, providing strong financial pillars to IIT Ropar.
24.5 CRÈCHE
Crèche (Day care) facility was started at IIT Ropar in September 2012 to take care of the
children of staff and faculty. The center caters to kids in the age group of 1 – 8 years and provides
the option of Full Day, Half Day and other need based services. The crèche facility is available
from 8:30 am – 6.00 pm, Monday – Friday. Crèche operates in an approximately 800 sqft. area
with a play den, kitchen, toilet and bedroom. It is also equipped with basic essentials like toys,
microwave oven, refrigerator, water filter, heating/cooling, TV, etc. to provide a safe and healthy
24. CAMPUS AMENITIES
IIT Ropar Annual Report 2014-1582
environment. Currently, there are two nannies to take care of kids and their needs. In addition to
ensuring timely meals and naps, the staffs of the centre keep the kids active and stimulated with
poem recitation, storytelling, drawing/coloring and playing with educational toys. Although
the number varies with time, an average of 10 – 12 kids use the facility. Since its inception, the
center has successfully grown to provide IIT Ropar parents with invaluable peace of mind when
it comes to their kids’ well-being!
24.6 CAFETERIA
The central cafeteria of IIT Ropar, located behind the admin block, is operated everyday from
8:00 am - 2:00 am to provide a nutritious, quality food service to the students, faculty and staff of
the institute at a reasonable cost. Our cafeteria is a relaxing space, enclosed by student painted
walls with views of the outdoors and lots of natural light. Seating in front of cafeteria provides
an opportunity to get closer to the nature under dense trees with a cup of tea or coffee. The
cafeteria is committed to provide healthier meals offering more fruits & vegetables, dairy
products and meat items. Each day, the users select from hot entries a variety of Indian and
western style entries fresh fruits and juices, cold drinks and cakes. To promote discussion and
student interaction outside the academics on national and international issues, the cafeteria
offers daily newspapers and magazines. We are continuously reviewing the entire line of
products and introducing new products so that users of all ages can be introduced to the
healthier foods.
24.7 TRANSPORT SERVICES
IIT Ropar purchased bus in September 2014 which runs between Mohali/Chandigarh to IIT
Ropar. This bus is used by faculty members and staff for their daily commute. It is additionally
used to take students to industrial visits. The bus is also used for similar services in the
weekends as well. IIT Ropar plans to offer more such facilities in the future, thereby catering to
the professional growth of faculty members, staff and students.
24.8 HORTICULTURE
The IIT Ropar transit campus is spread over 25 acres of land. Out of this approximately 15 acres
is green belt with huge lush green football field, cricket ground, athletics practice arena and a
park. Four gardeners are taking care of horticulture in the institute. In the campus there are 685
permanent trees of various varieties i.e. Ashoka (144), Silver Oak (69), Tuni (67), Eucalyptus
(56), Arjun (40), Persian Lilac (33), Gulmohar (31) etc. and 110 fruit trees of Mango (73), Guava
(17), Mulberry (9), Black Plum (9) and Peach (2). Very few trees yield fruit as of now as most of
trees are small. For the beautification of campus, 1292 flower plants were grown i.e. 118 Roses
of red, yellow, white, orange and pink colour, Marigold (225), Vinca (160), Balsam (140),
Hamelia (125), Zinnia (95), Cosmos (82), Kochiya(67), Kirondola (35), Salbia(28), Palmeriya
Alfa (20), Portulaca (20) and Dahlia (20) etc.

The Indian Institute of Technology Ropar (IIT Ropar) is one of the eight new IITs set up by the
Ministry of Human Resource Development (MHRD), Government of India, to expand and
enhance the quality of technical education in the country. The Ministry of Human Resource
Development (MHRD), Govt. of India, vide its Notification dated 09.05.2008 decided that the
Indian Institute of Technology Delhi would mentor the setting up of IIT Ropar. The foundation
th
stone of the Institute was laid on 24 February, 2009. IIT Ropar is registered as a Society under the
th
Societies' Registration Act 1860 on 29 July, 2008. The Institute is currently operating from a transit
campus, earlier occupied by the Government Polytechnic for Women. The transit campus was
th th
inaugurated on 19 August, 2009. On 20 August, 2009, the classes at transit campus commenced.
Professor M.K. Surappa joined as the first Director of the Institute on 10.06 2009, and Shri A.
Palanivel joined as the first Registrar on 10.07.2009.
IIT Ropar is committed to provide state-of-the-art technical education in a variety of fields and
also to facilitate transmission of knowledge in keeping with the latest developments in pedagogy.
These two areas of focus will enable students to gain exposure to recent trends in their chosen
domains of study and practical experience through a wide variety of activities that the Institute
facilitates in its own campus and arranges for collaboration with industry and other Institutes. At
the transit campus, arrangements have been made for classes, laboratories, hostels and faculty
accommodation. In due course of time, the Institute will shift to the main campus.
IIT Ropar is located at Rupnagar (formerly known as Ropar) town of district Rupnagar in Punjab.
th
Rupnagar was founded in the 11 century and was named after Rup Sen, son of Raja Rokeshar.
Recent excavations and explorations conducted at Rupnagar indicate that the first settlement here
were those of the Harappans, who reached the upper Satluj towards the close of the third
millennium B. C. The district has a rich historical and religious significance.
The town of Rupnagar, which is also the district headquarters, is at a distance of 42 kms from
Chandigarh, the state capital. Rupnagar is well connected by National Highway NH-21. The
Delhi-Ambala-Una railway line passes through Rupnagar and provides good rail connectivity.
The nearest airport is in Chandigarh which is located at a distance of about 50 kms.
The Government of Punjab has allocated 501 acres of land on the banks of the river Satluj to IIT
Ropar. When completed, the campus will be a self-contained township catering to all the needs of
faculty, staff and students.
At present, the Institute offers Bachelor of Technology (B. Tech.) programme in the following
disciplines: Computer Science and Engineering, Electrical Engineering and Mechanical
Engineering. This programme is spread over a period of eight semesters and the Institute admits
forty students in each branch. These students are selected through IIT Joint Entrance Examination
conducted every year. In addition, the Institute now offers doctoral programme in several
disciplines.

The overall academic system for IIT Ropar is designed to
provide science-based engineering education with a view to produce
quality engineers and scientists. The curriculum provides broad-
based knowledge and simultaneously builds a temper for life-long
learning and exploring. The undergraduate programme begins with
a set of science and general engineering courses which are reflected in
the course plan for the first year. These courses provide a foundation
for further discipline-specific topics.
Taking into account the needs of the curriculum, all facilities
and infrastructure are being upgraded. The Institute has been
actively involved in collaborative programmes with national and
international organisations/universities, to remain at the forefront of
scientific and technological development and to share the knowledge
for mutual benefits.
The Institute also undertakes a number of research and
consultancy projects sponsored by a wide spectrum of funding
agencies, including the Government and Industry. The Institute has
undertaken major research activities in areas of national importance
such as quantum optics and quantum control, low energy ion beam

The Institute provides facilities for research leading to the Degree of Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D).
The Research Scholares are provided Institute fellowship for pursuing their Ph.D. programme. The
areas of research are as follows :-
1. Quantum optics and quantum control
2. Low energy ion beam physics and materials modification
3. Polynomial representation of non-compact knots
4. Unknotting numbers
5. Surface Engineering and friction stir welding
6. Supra molecular synthesis and materials chemistry
7. Catalysis and Nano-chemistry
8. Modeling vitamin B 12
9. Bio-informatics
10. Archival research on history of education
11. History of political philosophy
12. Renewable energy
13. Heat transfer
14. Nanofluids
15. Material processing
16. Manufacturing
17. Micro-structure property relationship
18. Composites
19. Adaptive Signal processing
20. Wireless communication
The award of the Ph. D degree is awarded on the basis of satisfactory performance of a registered
candidate in prescribed course work, seminar and thesis submitted by the candidate and a final viva
voce. The thesis shall be the report of research work characterized by either discovery of new facts
or a new interpretation of known facts and theory, or an independent design or development of
new instrument/technology.

STUDENTS ACTIVITIESSTUDENTS ACTIVITIES
The academic year 2010-11 saw the creation of the Student Council that is henceforth expected to be
at the helm of all student activities at the Institute. The Council is expected to nurture the spirit of
sportsmanship and open participation in sports and cultural events.
Continuing with our past tradition students celebrated various festivals such as Holi and Diwali
with friends and faculty members. Everyone contributed to the celebrations so as to achieve overall
success of the festivities.
The idea of conducting a national level youth festival fest, together with hard work by all
culminated into a cultural extravaganza named Zeitgeist 2010 which saw significant participation
from educational institutes across the country. It was the biggest collective and participatory event
of the Institute with excellent participation from students of all entry batches. The cultural fiesta
included brilliant talent shows and contests involving music, dance, theatre and literary ventures,
among others.
The zeal and teamwork subsequently followed up in the form of the Inter Hostel Cultural
Championship - essentially an internal event of the Institute. Both festivals helped to raise
performance levels of all participating students, thereby inculcating a sense of confidence and joy.
The Institute successfully competed in the Inter-IIT Sports Meet held at IIT Delhi. Among the
participants, Naveen Kumar won a bronze medal for weightlifting in Under 77 kg. He was further
ranked second in Mr. IIT competition. The Institute soccer team won against the team representing
IIT Indore by a huge margin.
On the lines of IPL (Indian Premiere League) students of the Institute organized CricLeague an
intra-college cricket competition in which about 100 students participated. The tournament was a
huge success among the participating students.

CENTRAL LIBRARYCENTRAL LIBRARY
The Central Library functions as the primary information resource centre and repository of all printed
and e-resources for teaching and research activities at the Institute. Apart from textbooks and
recommended reading material prescribed for each course offered at the Institute, the library houses a
growing collection of research monographs, reports, multi-volume reference works, dictionaries,
encyclopedias, handbooks and so on. In addition, the library also facilitates access to a number of
journals through its participation in consortia, such as INDEST-AICTE. At present, users can consult
more than 7000 books (available on shelves) and thousands of electronic journals.
The library operations are automated using LIBSYS software and the library personnel are presently
working towards setting up a digital library and e-resource centre. These steps will greatly enhance the
library's efficiency in making the resources available to the academic community at large and also
enable the Institute participate in various inter-library initiatives at national and international levels.

A. Balance Sheet

A reference is invited to Significant Accounting Policy at Sl. no. I (Schedule 23)
which inter alia states that the financial slatements are prepared on the accrual basis ol

Above does not include expenses of7 2.44 crore pertaining to financial year 2021-22
but paid in April-May 2022. This has resulted in understatement of Current liabilities
and Provisions by7 2.44 crore as well as expenditure fbr the year by{ 2'44 crore.
B. Significant Accounting Policies (Schedule 23)
Accounting Policy (Schedule 23) al Sl.No. 5 states that expenditure on purchase of
chemicals, glassware, pubtication, stationery and other stores are accounted for as
revenue expenditure. This accounting policy is contradictory to the prescribed format
(Significant Accounting Policy at Sl. No.5) which provides that expenditure on
purchase of chemicals, glassware, publications and other stores is to be accounled as
revenue expenditure, except that the value of closing stocks held on 31 March is set up
as inventories by reducing the conesponding Revenue Expenditure on the basis of
information obtained from Departments. 'Ihey are valued at cost.
As a result of contradictory accounting policy adopted, valuation of stock at the end of
the year has not been done and value of stock has not been shown in the annual
accounts. No change has been made by the Institute in its accounting policy (Sl no.5)
regarding inventories despite being pointed out in the previous year SAR.
C. General
C.f Capital Work in Progress: t 619.07 crore
A reference is invited to Significant Accounting Policy at Sl. no. 4 (Schedule 23) which
states that in the case of commissioned assets. where all final settlement of bitls with
contractors is yet to be effected: capitalization is done on provisional basis subject to
necessary adj ustment in thc year offinal settlement.
Construction work of the Institute is being done through Govemment executing agency
CPWD. It has been observed that various works and buildings such as Administration
Block, Academic Blocks (3 Nos.), Residential Blocks, I lostel Blocks, Director
Residence etc. included in Phase-lA were completed and handed over to Institute on
30.12.2019 and are being utilized by the Institute since then. Similarly, various works
and buildings such as Boys Hostel (950 capacity), Girls Hostel (260 capacity), Type-5
(64 units), T-6 (8 units). Visitor Hostel (40 capacity), Library and Lecture Hall (600
capacity) etc. included in Phase-lB were completed and handed over to Institute on
16.08.2021 and are being utilised by the Institute since then.
The Institute is conducting its activities in these buildings. However, against the total
expenditure incuned on these buildings of 7 769.66 crore, the Institute has
transferred/capitalized an amount of < 436.30 crore only to F'ixed Assets up to
31.03.2022 and capitalization of works amounting to t 3i3.36 crore is still pending.
This has resulted in overstatement of Capital Work in Progress and understatement of
Fixed Assets by t 333.66 crore. Further, applicable depreciation for the years 2019-20,
2020-21 and 2021-22 is also to be charged on these completed works.
C.2 CapitalWork-in-Progress:Computer/Peripherals
NICSI: t 11.16 crore
The work of Networking in the Institute Buildings was awarded to the executing
agency National Informatics Centre Services Inc. (NICSD in February 2017 and the
project was at the closure state. NICSI had raised a demand for { 21.23 crore in respect
of this work against the payments amounting to { 19.87 crore released by the Institute.
which were booked in annual accounts as ComputeriPeripherals { 8.71 crore and
Capital Work-in-Progress { I l.l6 crore. The Institute has neither booked the liabitity
for balance amount of{ 1.36 crore payable toNICSI nor the fact has been disclosed in
the Notes to Accounts.
C.3 Records of Fixed Assets
Fixed Assets are to be recorded in the Fixed Assets Register as per the heads of F'ixed
Assets prescribed in the MTIRD/ Ministry of Education Format of accounls. It has been
observed that though the Fixed Assets Register was maintained but totals ofgross value
of these assets recorded therein were not made so as to match with figures of Gross
Block under various heads as appearing in the annual accounts. In the absence of
which, value ofassets as appearing in the accounts could not confirmed.
C.4 Ministry of Education vide OM No. F.No. l9-l/2017-lFD dated 23.2.2022
has clarified that each Bureau may issue separate notification for implementation of
Payment of Gratuity Acr. 1972 in respect of autonomous Bodies under their
administrative control. Annual Accounts for the year 2021-22, included an
accumulated provision amounting to { 9.45 crore in respect ofgratuity to the
employees, covered under NPS. However, gratuity can be given to the employees of

We have audited the Balance Sheet of Indian Institute of Technology, Ropar (Punjab) as at
31 March 2O2l,lncome & Expenditure Account and Receipts and Payments Account for the
year ended on that date under Section lg (2) of the comptroller & Auditor General's
(Duties, Powers & Conditions of Service) Act, l97l read with Section23 (2) of the Indian
Institute of Technology Act, 1961 as amended by Indian Institute of Technology
(Amendment) Act, 2012. These financial statements are the responsibility of the Institute's
management. Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements based
on our audit.
2. This Separate Audit Report contains the comments of the Comptroller & Auditor
General of India (CAG) on the accounting treatment only with regard to classification,
conformity with the best accounting practices, accounting standards and disclosure norms,
etc. Audit observations on financial transactions with regard to compliance with the Law,
Rules & Regulations (Propriety and Regularity) and efficiency-cum-performance aspects,
etc., if any, are reported through Inspection Reports/ CAG's Audit Reports separately.
3. We have conducted our audit in accordance with auditing standards generally
accepted in India. These standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain
reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements are free from material
misstatements. An audit includes examining, on a test basis, evidences supporting the
amounts and disclosure in the financial statements. An audit also includes assessing the
accounting principles used and significant estimates made by management, as well as
evaluating the overall presentation of financial statements. We believe that our audit
provides a reasonable basis for our opinion.
4. Based on our audit, we rePort that:
i) We have obtained all the information and explanations, which to the best of our
knowledge and belief were necessary for the purpose of our audit;
iD The Balance Sheet and Income and Expenditure Account/Receipts and Payments
Account dealt with by this Report have been drawn up in the format prescribed by the
Ministry of Human Resource Development, Government of India vide order No. 29-
412012-FD dated 17 April2015.

maintained by the Indian Institute of Technology, Ropar in so far as it appears from our
examination of such books.
iv) We further report that:
Balance Sheet

Designated Earmarked / Endowment Funds (Schedule 2): NIL
As per the prescribed format, earmarked funds are required to be set aside by educational
Institute for specific purpose. The expenditure on the objects, both Revenue and Capital are
deducted to the funds and balance is carried forward from time to time. Further, it states that any
other fund created with specific objects e.g. staff welfare fund, Pension fund also be included in
this schedule. The above does not include balances of funds of t 91.43 lakh (Benevolent
Fund:{1.64 lakh, Student Welfare Fund: <9.92lakh, Gymkhana Fee: < 79.87 lakh) which were
not depicted in Annual Accounts, but accounts were maintained separately. This has resulted in
understatement of Earmarked Funds, as well as Current Assets by t 9l .43 lakh.
Application of Funds

Buildings: < 270.49 crore.
Above did not include five buildings of < 61.49 crore which have been handed over to the
Institute during 2020-21, but have not been booked as additions under Fixed Assets. This has
resulted in understatement of Fixed Assets by T 60.26 crore, understatement of depreciation as
well as deficit by t I .23 crorc, and overstatement of Capital Work in Progress by t 61.49 crore.
Scientific & Laboratory Equipment
Above included four laboratory equipments of t 8.26 crore which have been received during
Financial Year 2020-21 but could not be installed upto 3l.O3.2O2L As the installation of the
equipments was pending, these should have been classified under Capital Work in progress as
per the MHRD Format of Accounts. This has resulted in understatement of Capital Work in
Progress by T 8.26 crore, overstatement of Scientific and Laboratory Equipments by t g.00 crore
(after depreciation of t 0.26 crore) and overstatement of depreciation by t 0.26 crore.

Laboratory equipment (DGX System)costing { 3.25 crore, for which payment has been made
during 2021-22, was received during Financial Year 2020-21. This equipment should have been

Consolidated Fund of India immediately after finalization of the accounts. Therefore, the same
should have been booked under Current Liabilities instead of booking it as Income. This has
resulted in overstatement of Income and understatement of Current liabilities and provision
(Schedule 3) by t 95.72\akh.

Accounting Policies (Schedule 23) Sl.No. 5 states that the inventory of chemical, glassware,
publication' stationery, and other stores are revenue expenditure. This accounting policy is
o contradictory to the prescribed format (Significant Accounting policy at Sl. No.5), expenditure on
purchase of chemicals, glassware, publications and other stores is accounted as revenue expenditure,
except that the value of closing stocks held on 3l March is set up as inventories by reducing the

valued at cost.
As a result of contradictory accounting policy adopted, valuation of stock at the end of the year has not
been done and value ofstock has not been shown in the annual accounts.

Special Features of the New Curriculum
The proposed B.Tech. curriculum will incorporate several special features designed to offer a unique
and enriched educational experience:

1. Emphasis on Undergraduate Research

Credit-based recognition shall be granted for the successful completion of outcomes from an
Undergraduate research project, thereby fostering early engagement in research activities.

2. Academic Credit for Startup Engagement

Undergraduate students shall be permitted to engage with startups, and their efforts will be formally
recognized through academic credits, which can be claimed under the mandated semester-long
internship requirement.

3. Formal Recognition of Leadership Roles

Student leadership roles, such as club management and the organization of major institutional
events, shall be formally acknowledged and credited within the academic structure to cultivate
essential professional and interpersonal skills.

4. Consolidation of Core Coursework

The majority of compulsory core courses are to be assimilated within the curriculum up to the fifth
semester. This structure will enable students to utilize the subsequent three semesters for in-depth
exploration of prospective career paths and engagement with a diverse range of elective courses.

5. Revision of Foundational Science Curricula

The foundational science courses (e.g., Physics, Chemistry, Biology) will be revised to ensure greater
contemporary relevance and applicability for undergraduate students across all academic
disciplines.

6. Program Clustering and General Engineering Curriculum

All undergraduate programs shall be categorized into clearly defined clusters (e.g., Mechanical
Sciences, Electrical & Electronics, Computing & Intelligence, Material & Chemical Sciences). The
General Engineering courses shall be distributed appropriately based on these established clusters.

7. Alignment with NEP Structure and Credit Framework

The Undergraduate program will be structured in accordance with the National Education Policy
(NEP) guidelines, comprising a total of 160 credits. This framework necessitates an increase in the
credit weightage for the internship and projects, alongside the formal integration of tutorials within
the credit structure.

8. Academic Credit for National/International Achievements
3

Academic credits shall be awarded to students who achieve exceptional distinction in national or
international events, thereby bringing commendation and recognition to the institute.

9. Provision for Exit Pathways

The curriculum shall be meticulously structured in compliance with the NEP and National Credit
Framework (NCrF) guidelines to incorporate multiple exit pathways from the four-year program.
The design ensures that students possess a requisite set of employable skills at each defined exit
point.

10. Integration of Online Coursework

A formal provision shall be established to allow students to undertake approved online courses as an
integral part of their course curriculum and subsequently claim academic credits for their successful
completion.

Curriculum Architecture
● Total Credits : The program consists of 160 credits, in alignment with NEP and NCrF
guidelines.
● Structural Framework
○ Year 1: Foundations
■ Mathematics I & II
■ Physics, & Chemistry for Engineers
■ General Engineering
■ Program core fundamentals
■ HSS (Communication/Ethics/IKS/Behavioral Studies/Self-development
and Literature)
■ Holistic Development (NSO/NSS/NCC, Life Skills)
○ Year 2: Core Consolidation
■ Mathematics III required by the program
■ Program Core Courses
■ HSS (Entrepreneurship, IKS, Economics, Behavioural Studies and Literature)
■ Beginning of program electives
○ Year 3: Flexibility & Depth
■ Program Electives
■ Open Electives
■ Minor/Specialization pathways
■ Capstone (Minor Project)
■ Internship
○ Year 4: Advanced Exploration
■ Open Electives
■ Major Project I & II
■ Advanced Mathematics/Science Electives
■ Research/Startup/Leadership credits

All compulsory core coursework is expected to be completed by the end of the fifth semester,
4
enabling academic flexibility in the final three semesters.

Remarks:
- At the end of 1st Year all 4 Divisions are completing 43.5 (21+22.5 | 20.5+23) Credits.

HSS Courses:
The HSS department will offer multiple courses for the first two years/four semesters, organized
under two buckets (one for each year) that includes IKS courses. The students will have the choice
to choose courses from these buckets. The courses in these buckets will be designed by the HSS
department. The thematic buckets will be clustered into two categories with specific concentration
priority for Year-1 and Year-2 respectively to match with the cognitive ability of the students at that
level.
1. All students will be required to undertake a total of 4 HSS courses (2 from Year-1 bucket
(HSS-1 & HSS-2) and 2 from Year-2 bucket (HSS-3 & HSS-4)).
2. The core capabilities priorities for Year -1 will be focused at developing interactional,
normative enquiry, basic analytical capacity, performing arts, and behavioral resilience.
3. The core capabilities priorities for Year -2 will be focused at enlarging the perspectives for
advanced analytical enquiry on society, culture, business & markets, entrepreneurial
thinking, and leadership ability.
4. The courses will be mapped with the thematic buckets (TBs), assuming one course will
contribute to many TBs.
5. Further, the HSS courses will have a flat course numbering system without any levels.

General Engineering Courses:
1. The compulsory General Engineering courses are limited to 10-12 credits in the first year.
2. The departments must make a choice between Workshop Practice and Tinkering Lab
courses in their program.
3. Other general engineering courses in the first year in the revised curriculum are:
a. Introduction to Computer Programming
b. Introduction to Data Science & AI (New Course)
4. Any other general engineering course(s) required by any B.Tech program and that needs to
be offered by another department should be made as part of the program core
requirements.
5. The demand of all such general engineering courses should be provided by the department
to the academic section so that the sequencing of the courses can be done in the overall
curriculum.
8
6. Further, the curriculum committee recommends removing the course code starting with
“GE” for the general engineering courses. Instead, the course code will have the prefix of the
department offering the courses such as EE201 “Signals and Systems" offered for CSE.

Open Electives:
1. A Btech program will have the flexibility to allow a maximum of 30 credits as Open Electives
to the students.
2. A student may take a maximum of 12 credits from a single department/discipline.
3. The department can also recoup a maximum of 12 credits from the open elective bucket to
fulfill the need to increase the overall program requirements.

Internship:
● Objective: Internship must aim to provide students with hands-on experience in
real-world environments, enabling them to apply classroom knowledge, develop
technical competencies, and understand practical nuances of technology.
● Types: Internship could be Industrial, Research or Entrepreneurial/start-up based.
● Timing: It is expected that the Internship would be typically carried out during
summer break after the 6th semester .
● Duration: The minimum duration of internship is 6 weeks.
● Assessment and Evaluation: The evaluation would include a presentation or viva
voce before a panel appointed by the department.
● Grades: The Internship of a student would be evaluated with a Pass/Fail grade.
● In exceptional cases, internships may be substituted with equivalent academic or
internal research projects (within institute), subject to approval by the Dean
Academics based on the recommendations of the Department UG Committee (DUC) .

Life-Skills I & II :
● These courses are designed to equip students with essential interpersonal, cognitive,
and behavioral skills required for personal success, well-being, and professional
growth.
● Students are free to choose their Life-Skills I & II courses from a bucket of courses in
different verticals.
● These courses will be offered and managed by the Students' Affairs section of the
institute.
● These courses will be a pass/ fail course without grading.
● These courses may include (but is not limited to) - Verbal, written, and presentation
skills, Emotional Intelligence and Self-Awareness, Ethics, Values, and Professional
Conduct, Financial and Digital Literacy, Self-defense, First-Aid, Legal Literacy,
Disaster Management, Public Speaking, Music, Dance, Theatre and more options can
be added from time to time.

Branch Change:
9
● Branch change will be done as per prevailing practice in the institute.
● All such courses completed in the first discipline, which are no longer part of the UG
program after the branch change, shall be considered towards the Open Elective
requirements of the students.

Credits for Tutorials:
1. In the new curriculum, Tutorials shall be treated as an integral instructional component and
included within the total credited contact hours of a course.
2. Updated credit structure calculation formula will be L-T-P-S-C:
a. C = L + T + P/2
b. S = 2*L - T + P/2
c. As a general norm, courses with L = 3 may include T = 1; however, this is not
binding.
3. Tutorials shall be designed to reinforce conceptual understanding through problem-solving,
discussion, and application-oriented exercises, rather than repetition of lecture content.
4. Tutorials shall be included primarily in analytically intensive or problem-solving-based
courses such as mathematics, core engineering sciences, and computational subjects.
5. Tutorial groups should be smaller than lecture groups to enable interaction, ideally
maintaining a student–instructor ratio conducive to active engagement.
6. Tutorials shall focus on:
a. Solving advanced and application-based problems
b. Addressing student misconceptions and doubts
c. Developing analytical and critical thinking skills
7. Tutorials shall not be used for syllabus coverage or introducing new theoretical content,
except for brief clarifications.
8. Each course with a tutorial component shall have a well-defined tutorial plan, including
topics, problem sets, and expected learning outcomes.
9. Tutorials shall include continuous assessment components, such as quizzes, assignments, or
in-class problem-solving, contributing to the overall course evaluation.
10. Adequate infrastructure and scheduling shall be ensured so that tutorial sessions are
conducted regularly and effectively.
11. Attendance and participation in tutorials may be considered as part of the course
evaluation.
12. Feedback from tutorial sessions shall be used to inform teaching pace and identify learning
gaps.
13. Courses without a strong problem-solving component should avoid including tutorials
merely to increase credits.

Minor and Major Projects:

1. Minor Project:
a. The minor project is expected to demonstrate the student’s ability to integrate,
apply, and validate learned concepts from the program coursework in a problem-
solving setting.
b. This project must act as a bridge between coursework and major projects,
10
encouraging exploration with more focus on implementation of known concepts.
c. This minor project must prepare students for Internships, Research projects and
Industry problem-solving.
d. The course template of the minor project for a Btech program must consider the
above mentioned points and formulate the execution of minor projects in the
same spirit.
e. The departments/disciplines are encouraged to come-up with design studios
wherein the minor project of the students can be hosted integrating different
aspects of the core-discipline in solving real-world problems.

2. Major Project:
a. In the 7th and 8th semesters, the students will have Major Project–I and Major
Project–II (as is the practice currently) respectively.
b. Major project I is of 5 credits while Major project II is of 6 credits.
c. Major project II is supposed to be a continuation of Major project I so that the
students could work continually on a year long project.
d. The students must submit a dissertation as part of the requirements of Major
Project-II.
e. The major project is expected to demonstrate the student’s readiness for
professional engineering practice or research, through independent problem
solving, sustained execution, and validated outcomes.
f. The students are expected to define a complex, open-ended engineering problem
with clear objectives and constraints as part of the Major project.
g. The problem taken up as a major project should not be pre-solved or trivial. There
should be a structured literature review to position the problem and identify gaps.
h. The students along with their project supervisors should be encouraged to take-up
the major project in collaboration with industry, research labs, or with other
institutions within or outside the country.

Credits for Online Courses
1. As per NEP guidelines, up-to 40% of the courses can be taken up in the online mode. For the
UG B.Tech. curriculum, the committee recommends the following:
2. A student can take up to 15 credits against the Program electives and Open electives of
the program as online courses
3. The courses to be taken online by the student need to be approved by the UG committee of
the department (DUC) and the HoD validating that the department will consider the credits
earned through the approved online courses and the mechanism of evaluation in the online
course is of acceptable standards.
4. The courses can only be taken up in online mode by a student if
a. Such a course is not floated in the institute and the UG committee of the department
and the HoD approves such a course.
b. Such a course is floated in the institute however the student is not resident in the
campus during that semester (for whatsoever reasons).
5. Courses offered via the open MooC platforms such as SWAYAM and NPTEL portals, subject
to the set of conditions are to be considered.
6. Online course credits would be counted against course requirements however these won't
11
be used in CGPA calculations.
7. These courses will be shown as Online Pass (OP)/Online Fail (OF) in the grade sheet.

Audit Courses
1. A student may apply for changing a credit course to an audit one within one week of the end
of the mid-semester examination. Audit is not allowed in any 1st year course and also for
any core course.
2. The audit courses will not be counted towards the final degree requirements.
3. The Letter grade for Audit courses will be:
a. AP (Audit Pass)
b. AF (Audit Fail)

Special Credit Provisions

1 - UG Research:
A student can claim a maximum up-to 6 credits (from the open elective credits) for taking up an
independent research project with a faculty member and with a published outcome at a venue of
repute.
1. Eligibility Conditions
a. The research must:
i. Be clearly distinct from Minor/Major projects and any credited coursework.
ii. Be conducted under a faculty member other than the student’s project
supervisor(s).
iii. Have evidence of sustained engagement (minimum 1 semester or 16 weeks).
b. Only peer-reviewed publications will be considered; predatory or non-indexed
venues are strictly disallowed.
c. The publication venue must be:
i. Indexed in Scopus / Web of Science / CORE-ranked (for CS) or equivalent (as
approved by the Department UG Committee).
ii. Classified as “Highly Competitive” based on acceptance rate, impact factor, or
ranking, as considered by the UG Committee of the department.
2. Credit Allocation
a. 6 credits if :
i. Student is first author and
ii. Provides a certified contribution statement signed by all co-authors and
supervisor ands
iii. Publication in a top-tier venue (A*/A category or equivalent).
b. 4 credits if:
i. Student is co-first author (equal contribution explicitly mentioned in
publication) and
ii. Same venue requirements as above.
c. 3 credits if:
i. Student is a co-author with demonstrable technical contribution, verified
through:
1. Contribution statement
2. Oral defense before a faculty panel under the UG Committee of the
12
department.
3. Note:
a. Credits can be awarded/claimed only after publication acceptance (not submission).
b. DUC will decide about awarding credits based on the evaluation

2 - Leadership
A student can claim a maximum up-to 6 credits (from the open elective credits) for verified
leadership roles in the institute subject to the recommendation of the Dean (SA) along with
respective faculty advisors of the student boards
1. If the student has served as the president of the student council then the student can claim 3
credits (only 1 student per academic year).
2. If the student has served as the general secretary of the boards (BOST, BOCA, BOSA, BOAA,
etc.) then the student can claim 2 credits (only 1 student/board per academic year)
3. If the student has served as the Overall Coordinator of the Tech/Cultural/Sports/Literary
Fests then the student can claim 2 credits (only 1 student/fest per academic year).
4. If the student has served at the leadership roles at different clubs then the students can
claim 1 credit.
5. Note:
a. Credits are not automatic; subject to evaluation by a committee regarding the
initiatives and the overall organization by the student.
b. No credits for nominal/ceremonial roles.

3 - Institute Representation
A student can claim a maximum up-to 6 credits (from the open elective credits) for exceptional
achievements by bringing laurels to the institute
1. Only recognized national/international competitions approved by the institute; the student
must provide the Official result certificates
2. If a student wins a gold medal in an individual sport/competition at national level including
Inter-IIT sports/tech/cultural meet then the student can claim 3 credits.
3. If a student wins a gold medal in a team sport at national level including Inter-IIT
sports/tech/cultural meet(s) then the student can claim 2 credits.
4. If a student represents the institute at international venues of repute (such as
ICPC/Laureate Forums, etc) then the student can claim 2 credits.
5. Note:
a. No credits for intra-college or low-tier competitions.

4 - Start-ups
A student can claim a maximum up-to 6 credits (from open elective credits) for a validated
entrepreneurial activity in the form of a start-up:
1. If the student incubates the start-up at TBIF and provides a demo of the viable product to
the UG committee of the department then the student can claim 3 credits. The student must
submit:
a. Business plan
b. Product demo
c. Financial and legal documentation
13
2. If the student incubates the start-up at TBIF, provides a demo of the viable product to the UG
committee of the department (DUC) and is able to raise external funding (value to be
determined by the UG committee) for the start-up with documentary proof or is able to show
revenue generation beyond a defined benchmark then the student can claim 6 credits.
3. Note:
a. The student can also take an additional internship of 6 months and work on their
start-up during this period as part of the additional internship i.e. 15 credits.

Remarks:
1. A student can claim a maximum of 12 credits from the overall Special Credit Provisions.
2. The transcript of the students will have separate mentions of the credits earned through
Special Credit Provisions for Research, Leadership, Representation and Entrepreneurship.
3. Any mis-representation of facts by a student to claim credits under the special credit
provisions will be treated as a case of academic misconduct and the case will be referred to
the academic disciplinary committee for appropriate action against the student.
4. In case of any disciplinary action against the student, no credit will be awarded under the
special provisions.

Department UG Committee (DUC)
For effective management of UG Programs at the department level, the curriculum committee
recommends the creation of the Department UG Committee (DUC). This shall be a 3-4 member
committee under the chairmanship of the HoD. This committee will collectively look into the issues
of the UG programs under the department, department level academic disciplinary cases, the Special
Credit Provisions, etc.

Multiple-Exit Options
As per the guidelines of the NEP and NCrF, the following exits programs can be considered:
1. Diploma in the Major Discipline : After earning minimum 80 credits
a. For example, Diploma in Mechanical Engineering, Diploma in Electrical Engineering
2. B.Sc. in the Major Discipline : After earning minimum 120 credits
a. For example, B.Sc. in Mechanical Engineering, B.Sc. in Electrical Engineering

Multiple-Entry Options
A student may re-enter the Btech program provided:
1 - the student exited the program with a Diploma (with minimum 80 credits) or B.Sc. (with
minimum 120 credits)
2 - the student makes an application to the institute for rejoining the program.
3 - the student’s application is evaluated by the concerned department (DUC) along with any further
evaluations to be conducted.
4 - The concerned department recommends the rejoining of the Btech program by the student

Minor Degree Programs
14
A student can earn a minor degree in a discipline (other than the primary major discipline of the
student) by earning 10% of the total program credits i.e. 15-16 credits as per NEP. Since the current
structure of minor degree programs is aligned with the NEP/NCrF, the committee recommends
continuation of the same.

Specialization Degree Programs
A student can earn a Specialization within the primary major discipline of the student by earning
10% of the total program credits i.e. 15/16 credits as per NEP. Since the current structure of minor
degree programs is aligned with the NEP/NCrF, the committee recommends continuation of the
same.

Interdisciplinary Dual-Degree Programs
A student can earn a dual major degree either in his own discipline or in another discipline (other than
the primary major discipline of the student) by completing 40 extra credits as per NEP. A department
may offer a dual degree option to the student with a requirement of 40 credits of course and project
works over a period of 1 year i.e. two semesters. Students can opt for this option by the end of 6th
Semester and must stay 1 extra year (5th year) in the institute to complete the requirements of the
Dual degree program. This option will allow students to earn a B.Tech in their parent discipline and an
M.Tech in an interdisciplinary area over a total of five years.
B.Tech students will have the option to upgrade to an Interdisciplinary Dual Degree
program after their 6th semester, provided they have a CGPA of 7.0 or above.

Suggested list of such Programs could be:
● Data Science
● Cyber-security
● Energy Systems
● Robotics & Autonomous Systems
● Quantum Science & Technology
● Complex Systems and Dynamics
● Cyber Physical Systems
● Electric Vehicles
● Tech MBA
● Quantitative Finance
● Public Policy
● Atmospheric and Climate Sciences

Course Assessment and Evaluations
Continuous assessment of the students is a fundamental pillar of the proposed new curriculum,
designed to provide comprehensive feedback on student learning progression and mastery of
course objectives, rather than relying solely on high-stakes, end-of-semester examinations. This
holistic approach ensures that evaluation is an ongoing process, encouraging consistent effort and
engagement throughout the academic term.

The assessment scheme for each course will be clearly defined in the course outline and typically
comprise a combination of formative and summative components. Formative assessments, which
15
are designed to monitor student learning and provide ongoing feedback, may include:
● Quizzes: Short, frequent checks on understanding of recent topics.
● Assignments/Homework: Problem sets or exercises requiring application of concepts.
● Tutorial Participation: Evaluation of engagement and contribution during small-group
discussions.
● Class Participation and Attendance: Assessment of active involvement and regular
presence in lectures and sessions.

Summative assessments, which evaluate student learning at the end of an instructional unit or term
by comparing it against a standard or benchmark, will typically include:
● Mid-Semester Examinations: Comprehensive tests covering material taught up to the
midpoint of the course.
● Project Work/Case Studies: Application-based tasks requiring research, analysis, and
synthesis of knowledge.
● Laboratory Reports/Practicals: Assessment of hands-on skills, data analysis, and
documentation in science or engineering courses.
● End-Semester Examinations: A final comprehensive assessment covering the entire course
material, usually weighted appropriately to reflect the accumulated learning.
The curriculum committee recommends up-to 50% weightage for Formative assessments
and up-to 50% weightage for Summative assessments in the compulsory core courses. The relative
weightage of these components will be determined by the Course Instructor(s) and approved by the
respective Departmental UG Committee (DUC), ensuring a balanced and fair evaluation. The
emphasis will be on assessing not only theoretical knowledge but also practical skills, critical
thinking, problem-solving abilities, and communication skills, aligning with the broader learning
outcomes of the new curriculum. Transparency in the assessment process is paramount with timely
feedback provided to students to facilitate their academic improvement.
It will be up-to the Course Instructor(s) to decide on the weightage distribution for the
non-compulsory courses such as department electives and open electives.

Schedule for the Implementation of the New Curriculum
- The new curriculum is slated to become operational from the incoming batch of students in
the 2026-2027 session.

Quality Assurance Structures
● Curriculum Review Board : Academic Council (UG)
● External & Industry Curriculum advisory board
● 5 year curriculum review cycle

IIT Ropar and Western Sydney University Join
Hands to Advance Smart Agriculture
IIT Ropar's ANNAM. AI initiative and the University of
Western Sydney (UWS) signed a Memorandum of Understanding
(MoU) and a joint work plan to establish a Center of Excellence in
Noida, marking a signiﬁcant step forward in India-Australia
collaboration in agricultural research.
The MoU was formalised in the presence of Mr. Jason
Clare, MP, Education Minister of Australia, and Prof. Rajeev Ahuja,
Director, IIT Ropar. The signing brought together two leading
institutions with a shared commitment of transforming agriculture
through science and technology.
The Joint Center of Excellence was conceived to work
across several critical areas, including AI-powered soil and crop
diagnostics, automation and robotics for farm operations, climate-
adaptive farming models, digital twins for agriculture, sustainable
water and nutrient management, and next-generation agri supply
chain analytics.
The collaboration brought together ANNAM.AI, IIT
Ropar's ﬂagship initiative in AI-enabled soil intelligence and
precision agriculture, with UWS's Hawkesbury Institute for the
Environment, which has an established global standing in
environmental and agricultural research.
Speaking at the signing ceremony, Prof. Rajeev Ahuja said
that the partnership represented a commitment to build one of the
world's most advanced agricultural intelligence ecosystems. Mr.
Jason Clare noted that India and Australia shared a common vision
for sustainable agriculture, and expressed conﬁdence that the joint
centre would accelerate innovation, strengthen academic ties, and
create meaningful impact for farming communities.
The partnership was widely seen as a concrete step
toward delivering research-backed, socially relevant solutions for
farmers, food security, and the broader agricultural sector.
Prof. Rajeev Ahuja Moderates Nobel Laureate
Panel at Quantum Horizons 2025
Prof. Rajeev Ahuja, Director, IIT Ropar, moderated a
prestigious Nobel Laureate Panel Discussion on Quantum
Materials and Intelligent Technologies at the International
Conference on "Quantum Horizons 2025: Materials, Intelligent
Technologies and Sustainable Futures."
The panel featured Prof. Moungi Bawendi, recipient of the
2023 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his groundbreaking work on

you the latest issue of our

IIT Ropar has scaled new heights

During these months, the institute formed several
collaborations with a single, steadfast goal: to advance research and
technological innovation in the global arena. To this end, we signed
MoUs with the Central Command and Western Command of the
Indian Army. This is a part of our unwavering commitment to
enrich our nation's defence technologies. Moreover, our
collaboration with institutions such as AIIMS Rishikesh, AIIMS
Bathinda, and Himachal Pradesh University opened up the
possibility of interdisciplinary research in key ﬁelds such as
sustainability healthcare and emerging technologies.
Apart from these, the institute also played a signiﬁcant
part in recent national conferences centered on industry-academia
overlap, like the National Industry Consortium Conference on
semiconductors and deep-tech innovation. Our dedication and
research potential were appreciated in several top academic-
industrial arenas, highlighting IIT Ropar's role in shaping India’s

As always, our achievements reﬂect the dedication of our
faculty, students, and staff, continuing to uphold the spirit of
excellence that deﬁnes IIT Ropar.
