"Unplugged: A Conversation with Aditya Kumar Sahu, Student Council President, 2024-25"

By the Maanjhi Editorial Team

We arrived at the BOST Room in the Utility Block expecting to find Aditya Kumar Sahu waiting with an empty space for our meeting and maybe some stale coffee, only to discover the space was already occupied by another meeting. Rather than interrupt, we found ourselves searching for an alternative venue — a familiar predicament that Sahu seemed to take in stride. "Hopefully, once the new council room is completed, we won't have to deal with these scheduling conflicts anymore," he mentioned as we considered our options.

Curious about this upcoming addition, we asked for more details about the council room he referenced. Sahu explained that the dance room currently under construction near UT circle would serve a dual purpose, functioning as both a performance space and a council meeting room, complete with its little kitchenette. It's the kind of multi-purpose planning that either works brilliantly or creates chaos, depending on whether the student government meetings coincide with dance practice. We ended up claiming a row of benches outside the now-closed Coffee Day outlet, the kind of impromptu interview setup that somehow feels more honest than any sterile conference room ever could.

Settling into our makeshift interview setup under the campus night lights, Sahu adjusted his position on the weathered bench. We got to talking, and when he asked about our upcoming endterms, we replied with all the enthusiasm of someone staring down a week of exams, Sahu chuckled knowingly. We ended up rambling about exam stress for a bit longer, which turned out to be the perfect icebreaker. When we finally got down to business, we began by asking him to look back on his four years of student life.

"I'm really happy with how these past four years have gone. I ended up with a solid friend group with people from all kinds of different backgrounds, and since good friendships mean a lot to me, I am grateful for my friends. Then, I consistently found opportunities to develop leadership, communication, and management skills—areas I had always been eager to explore—and I'm deeply grateful for those experiences. I've also secured a solid job offer, which gives me confidence that I'm well-positioned professionally. Overall, I can say that I'm content with my college experience."
"And looking back, how have you evolved during your time in college?"

Coming from a modest background, I had limited opportunities until 10th standard. When I began preparing for JEE, I had already mapped out what I wanted to accomplish during my college years. I set clear goals and worked systematically to shape myself around achieving them. My immediate priority was securing a decent job, after which I could pursue other aspirations.

I had always harboured a desire to contribute meaningfully to the student community, which led me to become actively involved in campus activities. I began by organising a fest (Advitiya 2024), developing comprehensive plans for it during my second year. Following this experience, I set a clear vision to become Student Council President. By then, my motivation was purely driven by a genuine desire to contribute rather than resume-building, especially since I had already secured a job. One of the reasons I chose to transition the student council responsibilities to my fourth year was to maintain a selfless approach to the role.

Through the Council, I cultivated essential interpersonal skills and gained valuable insights into how people think, respond, and perceive me—skills I deeply treasure.

I don't believe in pursuing activities without a clear purpose. As the first engineer in my family, simply being here represents a significant milestone. I carry no sense of entitlement or external pressure, only the weight of responsibility.

If I were to summarise my transformation over these four years, I would say this: "I've evolved from someone with potential to someone with purpose."

"Given that you're clearly someone who thinks ahead and sets goals, what are you planning for the future?"

My mother always taught me that we're born with a purpose, and it's up to us to define what that purpose is. I want to live authentically for myself while also dedicating part of my life to helping others. I'm not the type of person who claims "I'm going to heal the world"—I understand it's impossible to help everyone—but I want to make a difference within my capabilities, even if it only impacts one person at a time. I also have plans to start an NGO, which I know will be incredibly challenging, but I'm determined to make it happen. Above all, I want to always be there for my family, because ultimately, they're the driving force behind everything we strive to achieve in life.

We got into the more serious side of things now — his leadership role and how he felt he was handling it all. It seemed like the right time to move from talking about college life to discussing what it's really like being the one everyone looks to.

"What are the major tasks and achievements that you completed in coordination with the Student Council 2024-25?"

We kicked off our tenure with the successful execution of ISMP24. This was followed by flagship fests like Zeitgeist'24, General Championship (GC)25, Advitya'25, and Aarohan'25, each fostering community spirit, showcasing talent, and bringing students together in celebration.

One of the biggest achievements of the Student Council 2024–25 has been the creation of student-centric spaces, including the transformation of UT Circle into a Student Council Room, Dance Room, and Pantry (Epicure Room). We focused on improving convenience across campus by installing vending machines in all hostels, messes, and other key locations, as well as onboarding a new stationery vendor. Addressing student mobility, we successfully initiated PRTC buses to run from campus to Chandigarh and Mohali bus stands, increased the frequency of buses to Ropar, and secured approval to get the buses running on Sundays.

Recognising the need for better hangout and food spaces, we established new cafés like CSB and Bake O' Mocha and initiated the setup of a Verka booth within the campus.

To enhance hostel living, we enabled stable Wi-Fi in Brahmaputra Hostel, proposed an extension for better capacity of the Brahmaputra Boys hostel, initiated new common rooms, and added necessary equipment like Wheelchairs and Electric Pumps in all hostels. We kick-started efforts for a campus-wide E-Rickshaw service.

In the realm of sports and recreation, we oversaw the construction of the new Sports Pavilion, procured advanced sports equipment, and introduced Foosball and Pool tables for leisure. Our campus came alive with vibrant festivals and events throughout the year.

Finally, we ensured that IIT Ropar was actively represented at Inter-IIT meets in Tech, Culture, Sports, and Literature, took part in the Student Legislative Conclave 2025, and strengthened alumni relations through the successful organisation of the Alumni Meet in Bangalore'24.

"So about Advitiya 2024 that you organised—which was incredible. I think it had the highest participation we've ever seen. What's your take on why it was such a hit, especially under your leadership?"

The main thing I noticed was a lack of passion for technology, despite being at a premier technical institution. My priority became generating genuine excitement around tech, especially as we were organising a tech fest. We placed technology at the core and deliberately de-emphasised other aspects like cultural events.

We introduced on-the-spot prizes to boost participation—a strategy that had a tremendous impact. The vision resonated with the entire team, and everyone aligned toward one unified goal: conducting an exceptional fest. Everything fell into place once we prioritised technology and eliminated distractions.

"What challenged you the most in your role as president? And what's your proudest achievement so far?"

The biggest challenge was navigating relationships with vastly different personality types. Every day brought interactions with students, professors, and administrative staff—each group requiring different approaches. Managing that complexity was genuinely demanding.

My proudest achievement was the team we assembled. We built something resilient and succeeded in instilling genuine confidence among council members. That foundation will outlast any individual presidency.

"So, what are your expectations from your successor Xshitiz Chahal during his tenure?"

You know, when I think about leadership, it boils down to two key things - having a clear vision and being consistent in how you execute it. For Xshitiz coming in, I'm hoping he'll focus on keeping the momentum going with what we've already started. We've got some really exciting projects in the pipeline - the Verka booth, our new fruit shop, and the café - and these need someone who can see them through.

I think there's sometimes this pressure to come in and immediately launch a bunch of new initiatives to make your mark. But honestly? Just maintaining the momentum we've built and executing well on what's already in motion - that would be a huge win. If he can do that effectively, he'll have succeeded in a big way. Sometimes the best leadership isn't about starting something new, it's about taking what's working and making sure it keeps working even better.

"What did you do specifically for the girls on campus? And why do you think we see so few women running for student council positions?"

So one of the things I pushed for was getting sanitary pad disposal machines installed in the girls' hostel, plus making free sanitary pads available. It's one of those basic needs that shouldn't even be a question, you know? It's still in process, but I'm hoping it comes through soon.

As for why we don't see more girls in the student council, I mean our campus is like 80% guys to 20% girls, so the numbers are already skewed. But I think the bigger issue is that a lot of women just hesitate to put themselves out there. Some of them come from backgrounds where they never really had the chance to take on leadership roles before. Others worry that even if they do step up, people won't listen to what they have to say.

But here's the thing - leadership should be about who can do the job well, not about gender. And I'm excited that Harjas got elected as GS BOSA for the next term. She has earned that position. Hopefully, seeing her succeed will encourage more women to step up.

"So what's your take on what went down with the GC controversy?"

Look, I think people completely missed the point of what GC was supposed to be about. It was never meant to be this win-or-lose competition - that's such a narrow way to look at it. The whole idea behind GC was to bring everyone together, build that campus spirit, and make sure everyone feels included.

We put so much work into bringing GC back this year. Saksham, our GS BOHA, worked hard to conduct it. We had events running across all the boards, every club got involved. Everything was going smoothly, even though we had around 400 students participating.

But then what happened that day just... it's going to have consequences that last way beyond this year. Now the administration is probably sitting there thinking, "What if this happens again?" And that fear could seriously mess with future GCs or really any big campus event we want to do.

The whole thing could've been handled so much better if people had just thought it through. The situation could have been solved with a bit of maturity.

"We are a second-tier IIT, and there are things that need to be done to be at par with other major institutes, specifically IITs. What do you think our campus is missing when it comes to culture and infrastructure?"

You know, one of the biggest issues we face is how people around here actually see IIT Ropar. I mean, sure, the IIT tag means something across the country, but here in Ropar? Not so much. The local community just hasn't embraced us, and honestly, we haven't done a great job of integrating with the Punjabi culture around us either.

It feels like the locals see us more as...like we're just there to serve some purpose for them, rather than being actual partners in the community. And because of that disconnect, we end up getting the bare minimum when it comes to facilities and support.

I tried to push for some practical improvements - you know, stuff that would make life better on campus. Things like getting a proper café set up behind the chemistry block, expanding MaggiPoint, opening up CSB near SAB, getting vending machines installed — basic stuff. But it took me an entire year of work just to get these things moving, and some of them are still in process.

"So what's the story with your hostel room? Two presidents back-to-back - was this some kind of master plan you guys had?"

Not at all! It just worked out that way. Naviket and I became roommates in the second year. The whole presidency thing just kind of happened organically. It's just that the right opportunities came up at the right time, and we both just went for it.

I think what helped was that we've always had each other's backs. Like, we genuinely wanted to do something meaningful and make a real difference, and the student council ended up being the perfect way to channel that energy. It wasn't some calculated political move or anything - we just saw chances to contribute and took them. Just a coincidence.

"We noticed you always had this red diary with you when you started your term - what was that all about?"

Oh, that! Yeah, I love capturing ideas because they're just so... fleeting, you know? Like, you'll have this brilliant thought and then five minutes later it's completely gone. I couldn't stand the idea of losing something that might be useful.

Plus, I used it to keep track of all these little tasks and issues that people would bring up. Because something that seems minor to me might be a huge deal for someone else. I didn't want to be that person who just brushes off concerns because they seem small.

I tried doing all this on my phone at first, but it just felt clunky. But now I've got a phone with a stylus, which is way better - I can actually write, and it feels more satisfying.

"You've invested time in getting Maanjhi approved - why does this matter so much to you? And what's your advice as we try to move this forward?"

Honestly? It's because what you guys are doing is genuinely selfless, and that speaks to me. Your whole vision for this - it's real, it's meaningful.

I've had my fair share of disappointments. Projects that just died somewhere in the bureaucracy, proposals that got stuck in endless loops of "we'll look into it." But I don't regret any of it. All those experiences taught me things I couldn't have learned otherwise.

Here's what I've figured out - you need to understand what people need, not what you think they need. And then you have to get smart about how to help them get there. Sometimes initiatives can fail but you can't give up.

The important thing is— Stay honest with yourself, your family, with everyone you're working with. "Be completely uncompromising when it comes to ethics. Be transparent. Be fundamentally honest in everything you do." This will ultimately define you and your legacy.

title: Maanjhi - Your Campus Voice | IIT Ropar Student Publication
text:
Cricket, Campus, and Confidence: A Chat with Pritam Das, GS-BOSA 2024-2025

PRITAM! PRITAM! PRITAM! PRITAM! Loud cheering by the crowd...

That was how the journey of the most celebrated BOSA at IIT Ropar began. From the day of the elections to the day his tenure ended, the crowd has always shown love for Mr Pritam Das.

Having decided quite late to interview Pritam Das, we were glad that, in his true spontaneous fashion, he didn't think twice before jumping on board. However, with the vacation period underway, we had to shift the interview to online mode – not the most ideal setup, but the only feasible one at the moment. We shared the meeting link and eagerly waited for him to join. True to his punctual nature, he joined the meeting exactly on time – not a minute late, not a minute early.

The conversation began with pleasantries and questions about our own POR aspirations—a thoughtful gesture that immediately put us at ease. But as the dialogue deepened, we found ourselves transported through four years of transformation, from a carefree freshman to the leader who would redefine student engagement at IIT Ropar.

How were you as a student? Can you tell us something about each year in college?

My student life was nothing less than a roller coaster with loads of highs and lows... I came to college thinking I was signing up for four years of fun and freedom — no studies, no attendance worries. I dove into every club activity I could find, be it exploring music like learning the guitar, or dance, like giving Bhangra a shot. I tried everything. Though I couldn't go very far with either of them, I definitely found something more valuable–genuine friendships that would anchor me through everything that followed.

In my academic journey, the shift to offline classes was a wake-up call. Suddenly, CGPA wasn't just a number—it mattered. From that point on, I maintained a balance between fun and academics (even though studying was still limited to one night before the exams). One course that really tested me was Linear Algebra. With average marks around 15/60, the library became my second home—but I made it through.

Though the year was marked by academic struggles, it was the genuine friendships I discovered in the midst of all the chaos that made it truly unforgettable.

In the second year, two big highlights stand out. First was Inter-IIT—Pranav and I were the only two second-years selected for the cricket team, and that meant a lot. It was a fantastic experience. And then, of course, the elections. I've genuinely enjoyed the election phase all three years—it's thrilling. That year, we campaigned hard for a friend. Honestly, I got so caught up in the energy and excitement that I can't even remember half of what I said during the campaign!

The third year was quieter. I had an injury during Inter-IIT, which kept me from being too active. But those late-night group study sessions before exams? Definitely unforgettable. There's something about studying half-asleep with your friends that makes the stress bearable—and even fun.

And then in the fourth year came my most special and defining moment - becoming the General Secretary of BOSA 2024-25. Nothing could've beaten that.

"Although the screen was blank, you could feel the nostalgia in his voice as he recalled all these moments..."

How do you think you have changed in the last 4 years?

In school, I was that kid who never planned anything—I preferred winging it to structure. But college became a laboratory for discovering my potential.

The first two years were about exploration, trying everything available. Then I found my sweet spot: organising and planning events. That's when I realised where my true strengths lay.

I went from being impulsive and scattered to someone who could visualise goals, create detailed plans, and execute them effectively. It wasn't just about maturity—it was about finding my leadership voice.

Coming to your after-college life plans, what do you intend to do after leaving?

Software development is my calling. I want to spend a couple of years in the industry, building real-world experience. But studying abroad—particularly pursuing an MS in the US—has been a dream since childhood. The goal is to create a solid foundation first, then expand my horizons internationally.

"With his college journey well-documented, we could sense the anticipation building. It was time to delve into what he had called his most special and defining moment - his tenure as GS BOSA."

So, what pushed you to contest for the position of GS BOSA in the first place? Did you ever regret your decision?

It was my seniors. My life revolved around the council — watching and learning from inspiring seniors like Raghav bhaiya and Manik bhaiya, who were the President and General Secretary of BOSA for the 2021-22 session. Seeing them in action motivated me to stand for the elections myself.

I actually wanted to contest for GS BOSA in my third year, but I stepped back because my family didn't allow it. However, in the fourth year, I convinced my father and finally stood for the elections.

Regret the decision to become General Secretary of BOSA? Never. It has been an incredible journey that offers immense visibility and impact. You're part of meetings with councils from all IITs and are treated as part of the administration. You get to interact with juniors and fellow representatives, which really helps shape your personality, both as a student and as a leader.

A journey like this, full of learnings and joyful experiences, leaves no room for regrets.

How was your coordination with the other members of the Council?

As a team, I believe we shared excellent collaboration. Whenever someone put forward an idea or needed support, the rest of us were quick to step in and back each other up. Aditya Sahu, the President, working with him was a fantastic experience, and his dedication towards his job is noteworthy. Saksham Bansal, the General Secretary of BOHA, was incredibly supportive during all fests - Zeitgeist, Advitiya, and Aarohan. His efficiency in managing hostel and mess accommodations during these events was commendable.

Although we didn't have as much interaction with Dikshant (GS BOAA) and Amitoj (GS BOLA) due to the one-year gap. Every time we connected, the interaction was positive, and they both did an amazing job in their respective roles.

What were your main goals when you took over as GS, and how far did you reach to achieve them?

My primary goal was to increase student participation, especially among newcomers. I proposed hostel-wise competitions to get everyone involved, but due to overlapping activities and limited support from the administration, it couldn't be fully implemented.

Another key objective was improving access to information. We proposed a central bulletin board in the SAB to display updates about all BOSA activities. This goal was approved and will be implemented by the next council. While not every idea could take off, I'm confident that the groundwork we laid will benefit future councils and students alike.

We observe that Girls' participation in sports is comparatively less. What steps did you take to boost participation?

To encourage more girls to take part in sports, I proposed the formation of a Women's Sports Committee consisting of all female representatives. The plan included bi-weekly sports sessions exclusively for girls, along with a dedicated Women's Sports Day featuring events like kho-kho, dodgeball, and more.

Unfortunately, the proposal didn't receive full support from all representatives and the administration, so it couldn't be implemented. However, I genuinely hope the new GS BOSA, Harjas Kaur — herself a strong female representative — will carry this initiative forward and inspire greater participation among girls in sports.

What changes have you seen in the sports culture of our campus over the last 4 years?

Overall participation has increased, but there's a predictable pattern: enthusiasm peaks in the first year, then gradually declines as academic pressure mounts. Students start with incredible commitment—remote sports complex, coach availability issues, nothing deters them. But as internships and placements loom, priorities shift.

To tackle this challenge, it's important to strike a healthy balance between sports and academics. If committing 5-6 days a week to sports isn't feasible, scale it down to 2-3 days and free up time for studies. The key is to find out what rhythm works best for you.

Recently, we have heard of a rumour that Inter IIT sports will be held in our college in a few years. Is that true? If yes, what developments will be there in our college? And how would it help the sports culture of our college to grow?

Yes, it's true — IIT Ropar is likely to host the Inter-IIT Sports Meet, tentatively in 2028. While organizing such a large-scale event will come with its own set of challenges, preparations are already underway. We're discussing plans to construct a new sports complex with an Olympic-sized swimming pool, advanced sports facilities, and much more.

It's a massive opportunity, and if executed well, it could reshape the sports culture of IIT Ropar for years to come.

Speaking of Aarohan, we have seen the highest participation in Aarohan in the year 2025. As the Organiser of this sports fest, can you tell us some interesting inside stories and the challenges you faced?

This year's Aarohan was a wild ride—it really tested my patience. Those three days were absolutely sleepless. We had over 750 participants from outside the institute and a total footfall of around 900 students, the highest we've seen so far.

The biggest challenge? Accommodation. Around 450 students from three different colleges showed up at the same time, and some teams arrived as late as 2 or 3 AM. With limited rooms available, figuring out where to place everyone was hectic. Coordinating with teams in the middle of the night wasn't easy, and it honestly pushed me to my limits. But looking back, handling all that chaos taught me a lot about staying calm under pressure and making things work no matter what.

As we have been talking about sports now, you are known for cricket, right? So, when did you start learning cricket? What was your cricket journey on campus?

Cricket has been a part of my life since 5th grade; it's not just a hobby but a passion. I went through the Under-14 trials and got selected for the team.

My cricket journey faced a major setback in class 9 when I suffered a serious leg injury. In class 11, I tried to rekindle my cricketing ambitions, but my academics took a toll.

After securing a seat at this institution, I decided to revive that part of my life. The cricket ground at IIT Ropar was the first thing I looked up on the internet. I went to the ground on the very first day the coaches arrived, and I've been actively involved in cricket ever since.

Do you have a personal favourite innings in your cricket matches at IIT?

There would be quite a few. Like in a match against IIT Guwahati in Inter-IIT, where I batted for 14 to 15 overs, and we won that match. But my favourite would be a practice match against an outside team on our campus. During the match, I happened to glance at the scoreboard, and for a moment, it looked more like a phone number, with almost everyone stuck in single digits. However, I managed to score a solid 57 runs in that innings, and it ended with us winning the match. That was my favourite innings I've ever played.

So, coming to an interesting question. If your GS BOSA journey were a cricket match, what format would it be– Test, ODI or T20? What was your World Cup final moment in this journey?

I would describe my GS BOSA journey as a four-day Test match—a beautiful Test match. The first phase went smoothly, but the load gradually increased in the second phase with Inter-IIT. The third phase was all about Aarohan preparations—long hours of work and sleepless nights. Finally, the journey concluded with the felicitation ceremony—a perfect ending to an adventurous run.

The highlight—or my personal "World Cup final" moment—was that very ceremony, the felicitation. I received the loudest cheer. Even the Director looked surprised and whispered that the applause must've been because I owed everyone a party!

What kind of legacy do you hope to leave behind for your successors? What advice would you give to the next General Secretary or to students aspiring to take up leadership roles in sports?

I genuinely hope to leave behind a culture of greater student engagement in sports. I want to see our college rise in the Inter-IIT rankings and build a stronger presence in these competitions. In recent years, IIT Ropar has achieved respectable 7th and 9th positions, but there's definitely scope to aim higher in the coming years.

One challenge that continues to stand out is the low participation of girls in sports. I truly believe that with the new female GS BOSA taking charge, we'll see more representation, inspiration, and encouragement for girls to actively take part.

For students aspiring to take on leadership roles—especially in sports or cultural domains—my advice is simple: it's entirely possible to strike a balance and contribute meaningfully to both. With the right planning and time management, you can explore your interests and still excel. Ultimately, it's about how committed you are and how you choose to make it happen.

Even with the disconnect of video-off calls and virtual screens, we couldn't help but reflect on the journey we'd just witnessed. Pritam bhaiya had taken us through a journey that felt both personal and universal - the story of a student who figured out how to make the most of his college years.

text:
Diary of a Fresher

By Vaanya Gupta

Filled with darkness and gloom, misery and anguish, JEE felt like a storm that would never pass. Enclosed within the four walls of my room, I felt like a prisoner, my mom being the security guard, checking on me from time to time and slipping in meals. Countless books surrounded me, and my mind was the table bearing their weight. Even in sleep, I could not escape this darkness. Instead of hearty adventures and roller coaster rides, I dreamed of fast-ticking clocks, of faceless invigilators peering over my shoulder and of me getting buried under a pile of Physics Galaxy books and coaching modules.

There was no ray of light in my world filled with despair, except for one- one that radiated life, coming from the picture of the IITs that I had pasted on the wall in front of my desk. It shattered my bubble of gloom and took me back to my first day of JEE preparation- the day when I had promised myself that I would burn the midnight oil to reach my goal, and make my parents proud. I stared at that photo, and many mock tests later, here I was, standing in front of a real IIT - IIT Ropar. A weight lifted off my shoulders- I had qualified the JEE Advanced Exam with flying colours and my hard work had finally paid off.

My heart was heavy with emotions- fear, anxiety, curiosity and the best of them all, excitement. I was afraid of where this path would lead me, sad about leaving home, curious to explore what lay in front of me and excited- to finally get that freedom I had always longed for. My first goal from here onwards- to erase the word JEE from my mind, not as easy as it seems though..I am still working on it.

IIT Ropar- the IIT located within the lap of nature. My first encounter with nature took place when I got out of my car and our eyes met. It gently walked towards me and I ran back into the car, slamming its door shut- "That damn dog!". I am afraid of dogs, or rather used to be, as I am getting "familiar" with them now. However, IIT Ropar has a beautiful campus. Filled with greenery all around, with the sky changing colours every hour and a spectacular view of the lower Himalayas, I believe I truly have landed within the lap of nature. It has been only two months that I have been here and I have already spotted rainbows thrice- more than I have ever before. The infrastructure is no less, the most mesmerizing part being the entrance and the enormous SAB building standing tall on its foundations.

IIT Ropar is not just about scenic skies and grand buildings- it is about the vibrant life inside. On our very first day here, we realized that life here was beyond academics. We were no longer defined by our JEE ranks but by our talents and passions. I was awestruck to find out that there were so many clubs for me to choose from. I could finally pursue my interests instead of living a system-defined mechanical life.

The lectures sometimes feel like an endurance test—long, dragging hours where even the fan above seems to move faster than time itself. But unlike JEE coaching days, we now endure them with a different kind of patience—because we know that once the class ends, life outside the lecture hall begins. Whether it's rushing off to grab a snack with friends, playing sports, or just going for a stroll in the evenings, the fun that follows makes the boredom worth it.

The seniors have been so welcoming and cooperative, planning so many activities and club sessions for us to help us transition easily into college life. Our college days had started with the orientation sessions- yes, those long, monotonous speeches about discipline, attendance and how we were now 'adults'. If only they had mentioned the late-night maggi runs, the hostel jamming sessions, the freedom of roaming the campus with friends and the feeling of being alive again, I might have listened more carefully. We had Jamming Night, Cult Night, Janmashtami Celebrations, Fresher's Party, Garba Night and more- so many fun and enjoyable events within such a short span of time that we never realized that we are away from home. This campus has become our new home- the home where our heart lies and all our friends, teachers and staff feel like family.

Just when I had started believing that IIT life was all about freedom and fun, reality struck in the form of quizzes and mid-semester examinations. The library—usually quiet and half-empty—suddenly came alive on the nights before exams, filled with students watching YouTube lectures, desperately trying to make up for the 15 classes they had peacefully slept through. The real magic was how the night before an exam could turn even the most carefree student into a scholar, at least for a few hours. Right now, we are going through the silence after the storm- only this time, the thunder comes back each time our answer sheets are handed out.

Two months at IIT Ropar have shown me that college life is not really the picture-perfect dream I had imagined, and it is definitely not the prison I felt trapped in during JEE. It is a mixture of ups and downs, of boring lectures and beautiful sunsets, of reports and assignments that drain you, and friendships that save you. I have finally realized that life is not about living perfectly but about facing every challenge that comes your way with courage, laughter and lots of learning while making beautiful memories.

Between Promises and Progress: A Look at the General Body Meeting (13th September)

From Dubey Canteen's reopening to new hostel and sports updates, students shared ideas while the council outlined ongoing initiatives—and the campus looks ahead with optimism.

The First GBM of the Semester: Dialogue and Direction

The first General Body Meeting (GBM) of the semester was held on September 13. As expected, students raised questions about food, hostels, sports, academics, and transportation. The interaction offered students a platform to express their views, while the council shared progress updates and future proposals.

Dubey Canteen and Campus Food Facilities

One of the liveliest discussions revolved around the closure of the Dubey Canteen. Students emphasized the significance of affordable, protein-rich food options available on campus. The council explained that the temporary closure was due to pending tender renewals and staffing challenges. After productive discussions, services had resumed on a temporary basis. However, due to not meeting the set hygiene standards, it was recently shut down while a new vendor is being finalized.

Additionally, students provided feedback on the variety of food offerings and pricing, particularly regarding the night canteen. To gather more in-depth insights, a feedback form has been distributed, with assurances that the collected responses will guide transparent, data-driven improvements. Changes in pricing are still pending.

Exciting plans have been announced for a new food court between Ravi Hostel and Annapurna Mess, aiming to broaden and improve culinary choices on campus. Construction has already commenced, representing a significant advancement in enhancing campus dining facilities.

At the same time, the administration reaffirmed its commitment to reviewing mess rebate policies, which are currently under consideration by the mess committee.

Hostel Facilities and Services

The discussion on the Chenab hostel gates raised the issue of striking a balance between convenience and security. The council explained that, due to staffing limitations, not all gates can remain open simultaneously; however, efforts are being made to provide optimal access while maintaining safety and security.

Students also suggested reintroducing ironing and tailoring services—amenities that may be explored again depending on student demand.

Sports and Recreation: Updates in Progress

Under the Board of Sports Affairs (BoSA), several developments were highlighted. The new pavilion was undergoing final checks related to water systems before opening and has been inaugurated on 3rd November, while plans for new sports infrastructure, including indoor badminton courts and upgraded gym facilities, remain in the pipeline.
Space reallocation for upcoming hostels may temporarily affect some existing courts (volleyball and basketball courts outside Satluj hostel), but the council assured that alternative arrangements are being evaluated to ensure continuity in sports activities.

Academics: Flexibility and Support

Academic concerns focused on attendance, internships, and exams. Students discussed the 75% attendance requirement, pointing to other IITs that have adopted it. The council members pointed out that even at IITs with no attendance, exit quizzes are common as an alternative. They also noted that absenteeism can sometimes flag early mental health struggles, making attendance a tool for monitoring.

While removing attendance altogether seems unlikely, some flexibility was promised. Students representing the institute in competitions may soon be able to reschedule quizzes. Six-month internships were also clarified as possible with approval. Additionally, exam slot changes will be allowed in case of clashes—provided they're reported ahead of time.

Transportation and Security

Transportation remains a key area of coordination. Students reported a misalignment between current bus timings and train schedules, particularly with trains to Delhi, as well as the limited round-trip buses to Ropar. Along with acknowledgment, adjustments are being explored.

A proposal for paid campus parking was also discussed, aiming to strike a balance between flexibility for students and enhanced security.

Closing Thoughts

The GBM reflected the campus community's shared commitment to open dialogue and improvement. While some discussions focused on ongoing matters, the meeting's tone was one of collaboration and problem-solving.

Though held just before mid-semester exams, the GBM saw strong participation. Even without faculty presence, the meeting became a valuable space for dialogue between students and the council.

As the semester progresses, the community looks forward to seeing these initiatives come to fruition. Constructive discussions like these remain key to ensuring that campus life continues to evolve in response to student needs and institutional goals.

Until the next GBM, the focus stays on progress and partnership across all fronts.

CTC to RIP: A Fresher's View On Internship Season

By Lakshya Vajpayee

I am Yogesh, a first-year fresher at IIT Ropar. Been here for exactly five days. In that time, I've learned three important things:

The mess paneer can break a tooth.
The ceiling fan in my room has two speeds: "hurricane" and "emotional support breeze."
Seniors are... mysterious creatures.

Life was simple. Until today.

It started like any other day. I walked to the mess, humming the legendary fresher anthem "Where is my timetable?" holding my phone like it was a VIP pass to avoid any awkward small talk with strangers — and that's when it hit me.

The air was... different. Thick. Heavy. Almost like the oxygen had been replaced by coffee breaths.

Rows of third-year seniors sat hunched over their breakfast like first-years over new Wi-Fi passwords. Their eyes were bloodshot, their laptops open to spreadsheets, LinkedIn tabs, and chat windows with names like OA_final_final2 (do not share).

One guy leaned over to another and said, "You're good at OA." My ears perked up — OA? Overacting? I wondered if these people were part of some secret theatre club.

Another voice from the corner whispered, "CTC 43 LPA... base pay is only 12..." I blinked — CTC? Chuthey? Why would chuthey have a base pay? My brain was spiraling.

That's when it hit me. This wasn't the mess anymore. This was Internship Season.

To my left: a CSE senior, twitching as he hit "Submit" on an OA, muttering "Passed all test cases except the last hidden one..." like he'd just failed to defuse a bomb.

To my right: a mechanical senior reading HR questions from last year, his lips moving silently as if reciting prayers to the gods of Core Placement.

And then... they noticed me.

The Zombie Apocalypse Begins

One of them turned. His eyes were hollow but burning with desperation. "First year?" he asked.

I nodded.

Suddenly, thirty heads snapped toward me in perfect unison. Forks clattered. Mess chairs scraped.

"They have free time!" one hissed.

"They have SLEEP!" another wailed.

Before I could react, they surged forward like a tidal wave of unshaven faces and crumpled shirts. One tried to hand me a DSA problem. Another shoved a CV template at me. A third just screamed, "Leetcode! LEETCODEEEE!"

I ran.

The Escape Attempt

I burst out of the mess and sprinted toward the LHC. My lungs burned, my plate of paneer abandoned like a fallen comrade. The footsteps followed — slow, dragging, determined.

I ducked into a random room... and froze. Mock Interviews that's the first thing I saw entering the room written on the black board.

Two stone-faced seniors sat at the front, staring at me. "Introduce yourself," one barked.

I stammered, "I'm Yogesh... from Kanpur... and I like paneer?"

Silence. Then one of them scribbled something on his notepad and said, "You're hired."

I didn't wait to find out for what.

The Final Escape

I ran out, zig-zagging past more internship zombies. They were everywhere — on the stairs, in the courtyard, even hanging around the water cooler, discussing stipend vs. exposure.

A CSE senior shouted, "Wi-Fi speed is better there..."

And then... salvation.

They all turned, sniffing the air. Slowly, like a school of fish, they drifted toward the library. and they vanished inside.

I didn't waste a second. I sprinted back to my room, locked the door, and collapsed onto my bed, vowing never to enter the mess during Internship Season again.

Tomorrow, I'm ordering Maggi from the canteen.

Intro

Introduction:

Two years of countless studying hours, sleepless nights, unlimited problem solving and struggling to remember that periodic table for your JEE exam. Did you truly push yourself during that JEE marathon to get admission into one of the best engineering colleges of the country- an IIT? All those sleepless nights feel worth it when that allotment letter lands in your hands - got a seat at IIT Ropar.

You've heard the name. You've seen the rankings. Maybe you've dreamed about it, researched it, or wondered what life here would actually be like.You must have scrolled through that ranking list. But you actually feel the thrill while entering the gates of this esteemed institute when a sudden realisation strikes you then - "It's going to be my second home for the next four years". Stand at the entrance, and you'll see four towering 41-foot stone pillars-ancient guardians inspired by the Indus Valley Civilization that once thrived in this very region 5,000 years ago. These pillars don't just mark an entrance. They're a promise. A reminder that you're walking into a place where India's oldest wisdom meets its newest innovations, where history and future collide in the most beautiful way possible.

And the history and future being referred to here now?India? Definitely but also your past and your future self. Because when you leave from here, you're not the person you were when you arrived. You have changed to what you were meant to be. This is IIT Ropar. This is where your story doesn't just begin - it explodes into life.

Let us show you around.

About IIT Ropar:

Picture this, in 2008, among the limited IITs in the country, you suddenly see a new IIT coming up, that too in Punjab, but taking its first baby steps in Delhi. That's right, the Indian Institute of Technology Ropar, established as India's 15th IIT, started its journey as a guest at IIT Delhi (talk about having a good mentor!). This was the beginning of a new journey of a new IIT - a second generation IIT.

Establishing its identity in August 2008, where it started working from its transit campus in Rupnagar district, it finally took its first major step towards a permanent identity: the laying of its foundation stone for the 525 acre permanent campus on 24th February 2009. And what a canvas they had to work with! The land had a fascinating past: it once served as a detention camp during World War II. From a place of confinement to a hub of boundless innovation - now that's what we call a glow-up!

The campus entrance features four towering 41-foot stone pillars that pay homage to the ancient Indus Valley Civilization, which has deep historical roots in the Rupnagar region. Built in collaboration with the Archaeological Survey of India, these majestic pillars welcome you to a campus where past wisdom meets future technology. It's like walking through a portal that connects 5,000 years of Indian innovation! Now, let's talk about where the magic happens - the academic blocks that house our departments

The Brilliant Buildings Named After Scientific Legends

Each academic building is named after India's scientific luminaries—because if you're going to study, why not be inspired by greatness?

S. Ramanujan Block: Home to the Computer Science Department (where future tech wizards code their dreams)
J.C. Bose Block: Houses the Electrical Department (powering the nation's electrical engineers)
M. Visvesvaraya Block: The Administrative Block (where the magic of management happens)
Satish Dhawan Block: Mechanical Engineering's domain (engineering the future, one gear at a time)
S.S. Bhatnagar Block: Chemistry Block (where elements come together in perfect harmony)
Radhakrishnan Block: The Lecture Hall Complex (where knowledge flows like the nearby Sutlej)
Har Gobind Khorana Block: Also known as the Super Academic Block (SAB)—the newest star of the campus! This cutting-edge facility houses state-of-the-art laboratories and collaborative spaces
Nalanda Library: Your second home during exams, your sanctuary during all-nighters, and the place where you'll form a love-hate relationship with chemistry formulas at 4 AM. This place houses books for all subjects with facilities to help a student study during that hectic exam week.

Finally, one of the most important parts of your time here will be your home on campus—our hostels. IIT Ropar has several hostels named after the rivers of India. For boys, we haveBeas, Satluj, Chenab, and Brahmaputra(Boys), while the girls' hostels include Ravi, Brahmaputra (Girls) and T-6.

To make everyday life easier, the Utility Block is your go-to spot for snacks, stationery, and all the basic necessities you may need during your stay.

And what about those moments when you're absolutely done with mess food? Don't worry—we all have them. The campus offers several escape points: a Cafeteria with multiple food outlets, the ever-reliableMaggi Point, Amul, and Bake-O-Mocha to take care of your late-night cravings and keep you energized during long study sessions.

Lastly, when college life gets confusing, overwhelming, or simply chaotic, you're never alone. The Student Council, functioning under the seven boards of our campus, is always there to guide you, support you, and help you make the most of your time here.

The Seven Boards: Your Campus Support System

IIT Ropar has seven student-run boards that cover every aspect of campus life:

Board of Hostel Affairs (BoHA): Handles all hostel-related issues, from maintenance to room allocation
Board of Cultural Activities (BoCA): Manages cultural clubs and organizes Zeitgeist
Board of Sports Affairs (BoSA): Coordinates sports facilities, tournaments, and the annual Aarohan fest
Board of Wellness Affairs (BoWA): Provides mental health support through counselors and wellness programs
Board of Academic Affairs (BoAA): Addresses academic concerns and acts as a bridge between students and administration
Board of Science and Technology (BoST): Oversees tech clubs and organizes Advitiya
Board of Literary Affairs (BoLA): Runs literary clubs covering writing, debate, MUN, and quizzing

IIT Ropar has seven student-run boards that cover every aspect of campus life:

Board of Hostel Affairs (BoHA): Handles all hostel-related issues, from maintenance to room allocation
Board of Cultural Activities (BoCA): Manages cultural clubs and organizes Zeitgeist
Board of Sports Affairs (BoSA): Coordinates sports facilities, tournaments, and the annual Aarohan fest
Board of Wellness Affairs (BoWA): Provides mental health support through counselors and wellness programs
Board of Academic Affairs (BoAA): Addresses academic concerns and acts as a bridge between students and administration
Board of Science and Technology (BoST): Oversees tech clubs and organizes Advitiya
Board of Literary Affairs (BoLA): Runs literary clubs covering writing, debate, MUN, and quizzing

## Independent Clubs
Intro

Introduction:

Two years of countless studying hours, sleepless nights, unlimited problem solving and struggling to remember that periodic table for your JEE exam. Did you truly push yourself during that JEE marathon to get admission into one of the best engineering colleges of the country- an IIT? All those sleepless nights feel worth it when that allotment letter lands in your hands - got a seat at IIT Ropar.

You've heard the name. You've seen the rankings. Maybe you've dreamed about it, researched it, or wondered what life here would actually be like.You must have scrolled through that ranking list. But you actually feel the thrill while entering the gates of this esteemed institute when a sudden realisation strikes you then - "It's going to be my second home for the next four years". Stand at the entrance, and you'll see four towering 41-foot stone pillars-ancient guardians inspired by the Indus Valley Civilization that once thrived in this very region 5,000 years ago. These pillars don't just mark an entrance. They're a promise. A reminder that you're walking into a place where India's oldest wisdom meets its newest innovations, where history and future collide in the most beautiful way possible.

And the history and future being referred to here now?India? Definitely but also your past and your future self. Because when you leave from here, you're not the person you were when you arrived. You have changed to what you were meant to be. This is IIT Ropar. This is where your story doesn't just begin - it explodes into life.

Let us show you around.

About IIT Ropar:

Picture this, in 2008, among the limited IITs in the country, you suddenly see a new IIT coming up, that too in Punjab, but taking its first baby steps in Delhi. That's right, the Indian Institute of Technology Ropar, established as India's 15th IIT, started its journey as a guest at IIT Delhi (talk about having a good mentor!). This was the beginning of a new journey of a new IIT - a second generation IIT.

Establishing its identity in August 2008, where it started working from its transit campus in Rupnagar district, it finally took its first major step towards a permanent identity: the laying of its foundation stone for the 525 acre permanent campus on 24th February 2009. And what a canvas they had to work with! The land had a fascinating past: it once served as a detention camp during World War II. From a place of confinement to a hub of boundless innovation - now that's what we call a glow-up!

The campus entrance features four towering 41-foot stone pillars that pay homage to the ancient Indus Valley Civilization, which has deep historical roots in the Rupnagar region. Built in collaboration with the Archaeological Survey of India, these majestic pillars welcome you to a campus where past wisdom meets future technology. It's like walking through a portal that connects 5,000 years of Indian innovation! Now, let's talk about where the magic happens - the academic blocks that house our departments

The Brilliant Buildings Named After Scientific Legends

Each academic building is named after India's scientific luminaries—because if you're going to study, why not be inspired by greatness?

S. Ramanujan Block: Home to the Computer Science Department (where future tech wizards code their dreams)
J.C. Bose Block: Houses the Electrical Department (powering the nation's electrical engineers)
M. Visvesvaraya Block: The Administrative Block (where the magic of management happens)
Satish Dhawan Block: Mechanical Engineering's domain (engineering the future, one gear at a time)
S.S. Bhatnagar Block: Chemistry Block (where elements come together in perfect harmony)
Radhakrishnan Block: The Lecture Hall Complex (where knowledge flows like the nearby Sutlej)
Har Gobind Khorana Block: Also known as the Super Academic Block (SAB)—the newest star of the campus! This cutting-edge facility houses state-of-the-art laboratories and collaborative spaces
Nalanda Library: Your second home during exams, your sanctuary during all-nighters, and the place where you'll form a love-hate relationship with chemistry formulas at 4 AM. This place houses books for all subjects with facilities to help a student study during that hectic exam week.

Finally, one of the most important parts of your time here will be your home on campus—our hostels. IIT Ropar has several hostels named after the rivers of India. For boys, we haveBeas, Satluj, Chenab, and Brahmaputra(Boys), while the girls' hostels include Ravi, Brahmaputra (Girls) and T-6.

To make everyday life easier, the Utility Block is your go-to spot for snacks, stationery, and all the basic necessities you may need during your stay.

And what about those moments when you're absolutely done with mess food? Don't worry—we all have them. The campus offers several escape points: a Cafeteria with multiple food outlets, the ever-reliableMaggi Point, Amul, and Bake-O-Mocha to take care of your late-night cravings and keep you energized during long study sessions.

title: Maanjhi - Your Campus Voice | IIT Ropar Student Publication
text:
Surviving the Internship Season: My Story

Internship seasons can be tough, even for the strongest of us. And there's nothing to be embarrassed about if some (or in my case, most) of your friends got placed before you. We all take our own time to bloom. You know how in the same plant, each bud blossoms in its own time? The same thing happens here as well.

So, haven't gotten yourself an intern yet? Chin up, buttercup. You'll get there.

Hey there! I'm Palak, and today I'm going to share with you my experience of the college internship season. I'll keep it as real (and hopefully as fun) as possible. I'll share some hard truths, bust a few myths, and finally answer the one question everyone is curious about: what are your chances of bagging an intern when it's your turn?

How the Season Works

The internship drive is divided into three "days": Day 0, Day 1, and Day 2. Don't take the word day literally, these aren't 24-hour days, just how the CDPC (Career Development and Placement Cell) structures the whole season.

Day 0 is reserved for the big names: Google, Microsoft, and other top-paying companies.
Day 1 is for the second-highest tier of companies.
Day 2 is for the rest.

The hierarchy is obvious: the earlier your company comes, the bigger the package and the more competitive the process.

A Story from Day 0

Picture this: the night before your very first Day 0 Online Assessment. You and your friends are crammed into a room, laptops open, solving previous years' OA questions, brushing up on the "most important" topics, and tossing doubts at each other. There's nervous laughter, last-minute panic, and the quiet comfort of thinking you're all in this together.

But the truth is, even if you prepare side by side, one of you is going to perform better than the others. And this time, it wasn't you.

The next morning, you head to the CSE lab, nervous but also excited. Finally, it's time to test yourself.

But here's the catch: you're not a Codeforces expert who has been grinding since middle school. You only started coding seriously much later. One hour later, you walk out of that lab having solved zero questions. When your friends ask how many you solved, you lie. They nod, but deep down you can already sense the unspoken competition in the air.

And here's something that probably every one of you has heard stories about: How toxic the competition can get. Some friends won't share that one extra set of questions they got from a "secret" source that could've helped. You'll hear whispers about how a group of students sat together during the OA, and when you asked your friend to sit with you, they chose someone else instead. In that moment, you realise it's not just you versus the companies. Most of the time, it feels like you versus everyone else.

You leave with a heavy heart, maybe call your mum, dad, or sibling. They all tell you the same thing: It's just one OA. There will be more. Next time will be better.

You believe them.

But after failing the 3rd OA, frustration creeps in. You regret not starting preparation earlier. Still, you push forward.

Then comes the shortlist. You find out you didn't get selected for any interviews. Not one. On the big interview day, you watch your batchmates in crisp formals while the suit you bought proudly with your parents sits untouched in your suitcase. That stings.

You scroll through updates of who got selected. Some you expected, some completely unexpected. And here's something you only learn from someone who has lived through this: selections for interviews are often random. Not your OA score, not your CGPA, not even your resume. Just…random.

And even if you do get an interview, ace every question, communicate flawlessly, rejection is still a possibility. That's the reality of this system.

The Hard Truth

Here's the deal: internship season is, for most people, 90% luck and 10% skill. Of course, there are a few students so good, so prepared, that nothing can stop them from landing the top, highest-paying interns. They deserve every bit of it.

But for the rest of us, it's a game of odds. Sometimes you get lucky, sometimes you don't.

For Those Who Got In

Now, let's talk about the ones who do land an internship. Maybe you cracked Day 0 with flying colors, or maybe it was Day 1 or Day 2. Either way, hats off to you. You worked hard, prepared well, and your effort paid off.

But here's the thing, your story isn't just about the internship. It's about the countless hours you put in, the rejections you faced before the "yes," and the support system that kept you going. To you, it may feel like a personal victory, but to your friends who are still waiting, you become proof that it is possible. And trust me, that matters.

How to Deal With It

Now, here's my own personal advice for anyone stuck in that cycle of rejections and disappointments: give yourself permission to feel bad. Seriously. Decide beforehand, one or two days max, and let yourself drown in your sorrows. Stay in bed, cry it out if you need to, binge-watch that comfort movie, or go eat your favorite food at that one restaurant that always cheers you up.

But once those two days are over? Whether you want to or not, get your ass back to studying and preparing. No excuses. The only way forward is through.

Where We Stand

The truth is, surviving internship season isn't just about landing an offer. It's about resilience, patience, and getting back up no matter how many times you're pushed down.

Whether you're a senior still in the middle of the process or a junior preparing for your turn, remember this: the internship season does not define your worth, your skills, or your future. It's just one chapter in a much bigger story.

Some people bloom on Day 0, some on Day 1, some later, and some even outside this system altogether. But bloom you will. Your opportunity will come, in its own time and in its own way. And when it does? That untouched suit in your suitcase will finally get its day.

Fun fact before I sign off: 70 students got an intern during Day 0. So, shoutout to CDPC for making it happen.

THE BROKE STUDENT GUIDE

How to Live Like Royalty on a Budget That Couldn't Buy a Dairy Milk

Welcome, financially fragile fresher or miserably broke final-yearite.

If your wallet echoes like an empty tunnel and your UPI balance rarely crosses ₹0.00, this guide is your holy scripture. Blessed are the broke, for they shall find... birthday parties with free cake.

In the grand tradition of survival literature, we present the definitive guide to being broke in college and still living like a legend.

The Mess-tastic Survival Strategy

The mess: where taste goes to die but survival is assured.

Your cravings may scream for Zomato, but remember — mess food is already paid for.

Breakfast? Take two bananas for "later."
Lunch? Mix daal and curd — boom, free kadhi.
Dinner? Befriend the mess staff. Smile like your GPA depends on that extra chapati. (It does)

You don't eat for the flavor — you eat for the financial liberation.

The Pen Piracy Program

Pens are public property.

Need a pen?

Step 1: Walk into the library.

Step 2: Spot one abandoned on a desk.

Step 3: Walk out like an intellectual James Bond.

Birthday Parties

You don't need to be invited.

Just follow the sound of balloons and the scent of Domino's.

Pro tip: Say "Happy Birthday, bro!" to whoever's holding a knife near a cake.

No one questions free enthusiasm — and you walk away with cake, coke, and sometimes even leftover garlic bread.

Shampoo Economics

Who needs personal hygiene products when you have roommates?

Borrow shampoo like it's a UN peace treaty.

Bonus trick: Use that tiny amount left in a nearly empty bottle, add water, shake = shampoo smoothie.

Science wins.

The Art of Recycling Clothes

Wearing the same outfit for three days isn't gross — it's sustainable fashion.

Rotate three T-shirts like a washing machine stuck in "eco" mode.

Laundry once a week. Underwear inside out on Day 2. We don't talk about Day 3.

The Notebook Negotiation

Notebooks are priced like luxury goods. If you're down to the last few pages, start writing sideways. Borrow unused last pages from friends' lab notebooks like you're harvesting communal crops.

When desperate, photocopy your friend's notebook — tell them it's for "backup." Or better yet, join the Drawing Club — they have more paper than a stationery store. Just make sure no one notices you're writing thermodynamics on a sheet meant for a sketch of a tree.

How to Emotionally Manipulate Your Wallet

Every time you want to splurge, stare at your bank balance and whisper:

"Would my future self approve of this ₹40 paneer wrap?"

Then silently eat the banana you stole from breakfast.

Delayed gratification. Mild sadness. Long-term financial triumph.

Advanced Techniques

If you're truly committed to mastering the broke life, here are expert-level hacks:

• Join Epicure, the food club on campus. Not for culinary passion, but for tasting sessions. Sign up once, eat forever. Bonus: pretend you're a food critic while devouring free pastries.
• Volunteer at campus events — collect free T-shirts and food tokens like rare Pokémon.
• Attend department seminars for the "knowledge," but stay for the samosas.
• Crash hostel parties hosted by rich kids. Say you're a friend of a friend. Smile. Eat. Leave.

You don't need a fat wallet to live a full life in college.

You need hustle. You need charm. You need the courage to call Maggi a "balanced meal."

So here's to all the broke students — smart, scrappy, and slightly hungry. You don't survive college in style despite being broke.

You survive in style because you're broke.

Congratulations. That's ₹5 saved. You're basically an investor now.

EDUROAM
About eduroam

IIT Ropar is a participant in eduroam, a secure, worldwide Wi-Fi roaming service for the international research and education community. In India, eduroam is facilitated by ERNET India.

With eduroam, students, faculty, and staff can securely access internet connectivity at participating institutions worldwide using the SSID eduroam, without the need for separate credentials at each location.

User authentication is performed through the institute’s authentication system using LDAP and RADIUS services. Visitors from other eduroam-enabled institutions can also connect using the credentials provided by their home organization.

Eduroam is currently available in over 100 countries, providing seamless and secure connectivity across thousands of academic and research institutions globally.

title: Aarohan 2025
text:
Athletics

Athletics covers a range of track and field events, including sprinting, long-distance running, jumping, and throwing. The sport is a key part of the Olympic Games and showcases incredible physical endurance and skill.

Basketball

Basketball is a high-energy sport played on a court, where players aim to score points by shooting a ball through a hoop. The NBA is one of the most followed leagues globally.

Badminton

Badminton is a racquet sport played with a shuttlecock. It is popular for its fast-paced action and requires excellent reflexes and precision. International events like the All England Open attract global attention.

Chess

Chess is a strategic board game played by millions around the world. It challenges the mind with tactical moves and long-term planning. Competitions like the Chess Olympiad and World Championship are highly celebrated.

Cricket

Cricket is a bat-and-ball game with global appeal, especially in countries like India, Australia, and England. The game has various formats, from Test cricket to the fast-paced T20 matches.

Football

Football is a fast-paced game that involves teamwork, strategy, and athleticism. It is one of the most popular sports worldwide, with leagues like the NFL and FIFA World Cup attracting millions of fans.

Hockey

Hockey is an exciting team sport played on grass or ice, requiring speed, agility, and skill. Competitions like the Hockey World Cup and Olympics are widely followed by fans.

Weightlifting

Weightlifting and powerlifting are strength sports that test athletes ability to lift heavy weights. These events are a staple in international competitions like the Olympics.

Table Tennis

Table Tennis, also known as ping pong, is a fast-paced sport that requires quick reflexes and precision. It is played both recreationally and competitively worldwide.

Tennis

Tennis is a racket sport played individually or in doubles, featuring intense rallies and strategic play. Grand Slam tournaments like Wimbledon and the US Open are highly prestigious events.

Volleyball

Volleyball is a dynamic team sport where players aim to score points by hitting the ball over a net into the opposing teams court. It is played both indoors and on the beach.
